activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: A useful way to predict temperature effects is to treat heat as a product of an exothermic reaction and as a reactant of an endothermic one.
story:
Sienna had promised herself she would understand the blue tubes before the field trip ended, and now there were twenty minutes left. The exhibit hall smelled of hand sanitizer and carpet dust, and behind the glass a sealed tube held two gases that kept turning into each other, brown and colorless, colorless and brown, like an argument neither side could win. Ms. Nikolaidis had set a quiz for Monday: predict which way a reaction shifts when you heat it. Sienna had gotten the first three questions wrong in a row, the same wrong direction each time, which felt less like a mistake and more like something congenital in her thinking, a built-in flaw she couldn't locate.

Lana and Tristan were at the wall of push-button demonstrations, Tristan mashing a button that launched a pneumatic rocket into netting. "Come look at this one," Lana called, but Sienna stayed at the tube. There was a heating element below the glass and a cooling plate above it, and a placard that said only: N2O4, NO2, equilibrium, without giving away which way anything moved. Typical. The museum wanted you to feel wonder; it did not want you to pass Chemistry.

She crouched and pressed her palm flat against the warm glass near the element. Heat was going in. Last weekend, at her grandmother's apartment, she had spread her homework across the kitchen table while her grandmother shelled peas and asked what the equations meant. Sienna hadn't been able to say. Her grandmother had only finished the eighth grade, and Sienna, who could recite molarity formulas in her sleep, had discovered she could not explain a single one of them out loud, which made her feel like a dilettante, a collector of procedures with nothing underneath.

The placard's graph showed concentration against time, two curves braiding toward flatness. When the tube warmed, the brown gas thickened; when it cooled, the mixture went pale. Brown was NO2, the graph said. So heating made more NO2. Fine, but the quiz questions had arrows and delta-H values, no colors, and she kept choosing the wrong side.

Then it arrived, the way her grandmother said answers arrived when you were shelling peas: not as information but as rearrangement. She took out her notebook and wrote the equation from Sunday's problem, the exothermic one, the one she'd missed. Then, in pencil, on the products side, she wrote the word heat, as if heat were just another substance the reaction made. If heat was a product, then adding heat was like adding product, and everything she knew about adding product came back to her at once: the reaction runs backward, consumes it, shifts left. That's why her answer had been wrong. And the endothermic ones, she wrote heat on the reactants' side, and adding heat there meant feeding the forward reaction, shift right. She sat back on her heels. "Lana. Come here."

Lana crouched beside her, still holding a rubber rocket Tristan had handed her for reasons of his own. Sienna showed her the notebook, the word heat penciled into both equations. "So heat is a product of an exothermic reaction," Lana read slowly, "and a reactant of an endothermic one." She looked up. "You just invented that?" "It's not invented if it works," Sienna said, but her voice wobbled, because she wasn't sure it worked. It worked for the tube. It worked for Sunday's problem, retroactively, in a way that felt like the problem transfigured, the same marks on paper suddenly meaning something. But she had no idea whether it was a rule or a trick, whether a teacher would circle the word heat in red and write not a substance across it.

"Ask Nikolaidis," Lana said. Ms. Nikolaidis was by the Foucault pendulum, half-listening to Tristan argue that the pendulum proved the earth spun but not that it was round. Sienna approached her with the notebook open, feeling the way she'd felt at her grandmother's table, like explaining would be the real test. "I wrote heat into the equations," she said. "As a product or a reactant. Is that allowed, or did I just make something up?" Ms. Nikolaidis read the page for a long moment, long enough that Sienna's ears went hot.

"Where did you get that?" she asked finally, and Sienna braced for the red-pen answer. "Nowhere. The tube, and the graph, and I wrote it in." Ms. Nikolaidis closed the notebook and handed it back. "It's a useful way to predict temperature effects," she said. "People teach it." Sienna exhaled so hard that Tristan, arriving, asked if she was okay. She was more than okay; she had found something true on her own, or nearly on her own, and the nearly was the part that felt important, the part she'd want to say out loud someday, that she still didn't know why it worked, only that it did.

On the bus back, she leaned against the window with the notebook on her knees and worked the remaining quiz questions, all of them, even the ones due weeks ahead. Tristan leaned over the seat. "You know she's going to mark it wrong if you literally write the word heat into the equation." Sienna looked down at the page, where her penciled heat sat tucked beside the products of the very first problem, and realized she had no intention of erasing it. "Then I'll write it in pen," she said, and clicked the pen, and began.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: When entering a highway, drivers use the acceleration lane to reach a speed close to that of highway traffic before merging, since merging slowly forces others to brake.
story:
Rose had parallel parking down to a ritual: line the mirror up with the cone, full lock, count to three, straighten, back in, celebrate. She could do it in her sleep, and sometimes did, dreaming of cones arranged like patient jurors. What she could not do was merge. The on-ramp near the driving school rose in a long curve toward the highway, and every time Mr. Ricci said "Okay, your merge," something in her chest went quiet and cold, like a radio losing its station.

"It's not the steering," Marika said, watching from the back seat during their shared lesson. "You steer fine. You just go up that ramp like you're approaching a church."

"Maybe I'm religious," Rose said. "About surviving."

Marika's brother had been driving for two years and had opinions he shared at family dinners, which Marika relayed like foreign dispatches. On this particular Tuesday the dispatch was about ramps. "He says the acceleration lane is for getting up to the speed of highway traffic before you merge. If you come in slow, everyone behind you has to brake." She said it the way she reported most of her brother's wisdom, eyebrows raised, as if to ask whether Rose found it as obvious as he clearly had.

Rose found it not obvious at all. Her whole instinct said slow was safe, that caution was a virtue you could apply uniformly, like sunscreen. Slowing down near other cars felt polite. The idea that speed could be the courtesy, that entering a highway timidly made things worse for everyone, sat strangely in her mind, next to a memory of her mother inching the family car down the grocery aisle at walking pace, one hand hovering over the horn as if the horn were the problem.

She tested it anyway, because Mr. Ricci had a rule: every fear had to be attempted at least twice before it could be complained about. The first attempt she hedged, holding at fifty while the highway traffic poured past at highway speed, and the pickup behind her had to brake, headlights dipping once, darkly, like a man shaking his head. She felt it in her stomach before she understood it: the slowness had caused the danger. The second attempt she pressed the accelerator through the curve, the engine note climbing, the fence posts flicking past, and when she merged the nearest car barely lifted its front end, and there was a gap where she was supposed to be, exactly her size, as if the highway had been holding her place.

"That," said Marika from the back, "was almost sexy."

"It was adequate," said Mr. Ricci, which from him was a parade.

Afterward, sitting on the curb outside the school eating fries from the place next door, Rose tried to explain to Aliya what she'd figured out, and found it harder than the driving. "It's like, everything I was taught is about slowing down near danger. But the highway is the opposite. You commit. You match them." The evening light was doing something evanescent to the parking lot, turning the oil stains briefly gold, and she thought about how all of this, the cones and the fries and even the fear, would dissolve that way, quickly, and be gone before anyone agreed on what it had meant.

"Or," said Aliya, "it's one system, and you just learned which lane you were in."

"That's suspiciously wise for someone who failed her written test twice."

"The second time was a clerical error. The system is in a state of total entropy and I am its victim."

Test day arrived hot and bright, the parking lot of the examination centre shimmering faintly, cones set out in their familiar judgmental row. The examiner was a small woman with reading glasses on a chain and the demeanor of someone who had seen four decades of teenagers approach her clipboard like it was a customs border. Rose parallel parked first, smooth as pouring cream, and the examiner made a small mark. Then the highway. The ramp rose, the traffic poured, and Rose did not go quiet and cold. She accelerated through the curve, matched the flow, slid into the gap, signalled off again four exits later, everything clean, and returned to the centre certain, for one whole minute, that she had it.

The examiner made another small mark and did not look up. "You'll have to come back," she said. "You did everything well. But you were over the limit the entire time on the acceleration lane." She turned the clipboard around so Rose could see it. "Getting up to highway speed is one thing, dear. Nineteen over is another."

Behind the glass doors, Marika lifted her fries in a slow, solemn salute.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In soccer, being in an offside position is not an offence by itself; a player is penalized only when involved in active play, and there is no offside from a throw-in, goal kick or corner.
story:
The bleachers at the community field smelled like cut grass and someone's burnt hot dogs, and Paige had claimed the third row because from there she could see both goals without the sun in her eyes. Her uncle had arrived late, as he always did, carrying a folding chair he never unfolded, and he planted himself two rows below her so that every complaint he made rose directly into her space. Tala sat on her left with a laminated schedule she'd annotated in three colors, and Klara was somewhere below, working the snack table because she'd decided, that spring, that she could make more money selling lemonade than watching games ever earned her anything.

Paige had come mostly because Tala wanted her there. Tala played on the community team and had spent two weeks lobbying Paige to try out for the fall squad, pointing out that Paige had good instincts, whatever that meant, and that the team needed a defender who actually read the field instead of chasing the ball. Paige had said maybe. She'd said maybe four times now, each time with slightly less conviction, because the truth was she liked watching soccer more than she liked playing it, and she hadn't figured out whether that was a failing or just a preference.

The game was tied one to one in the second half, and the boreal wind that came off the far treeline whenever the clouds opened kept lifting napkins off the bleacher steps in little spirals. Paige had her mother's old rulebook app on her phone, half out of curiosity and half because she liked knowing how the machinery of a game worked underneath the shouting. She'd been reading about restarts during a slow stretch when the corner came.

The ball swung in low, skimmed off two defenders, and the striker nobody had been marking buried it near post. The crowd around Paige erupted, and her uncle was on his feet before the net had stopped shaking, pointing at the striker and then at the linesman.

"He was offside! He was three meters behind the last man, look at him, he never came back!"

The referee, a neighbor everyone knew as Mr. Wardak, jogged toward the sideline, and Paige watched the assistant keep his flag down, arms folded, entirely unbothered. Her uncle kept shouting, and a few people near him took it up, a low grumble of offside, offside, moving through the stands like the wind moving the napkins.

"Goal stands," the announcer said over the speaker, and Mr. Wardak turned toward the bleachers, calm, almost polite. "No offside from a corner, sir." He said it once, without heat, and turned back to the game.

Her uncle sat down muttering, but Paige was already scrolling. Tala leaned over her shoulder. "What are you looking for?"

"Whether he's right," Paige said. "Whether it's just corners, or whether it's the whole rule I've been misunderstanding." Because she had always thought, without ever examining the thought, that offside was like a line you crossed, a place you stood, a sin committed by geography alone. The rulebook said otherwise. She found the passage and read it twice, mouthing it.

"Listen to this," she said. "Being in an offside position isn't an offence by itself. You only get penalized if you get involved in active play. So he could stand behind the whole defense all day, and it's nothing, until the ball comes to him."

"So what counts as involved?" Tala took the phone and scrolled, frowning at the dense text like it was a physics problem she intended to beat.

Paige kept reading over her arm. "And there's no offside from a throw-in either. Or a goal kick. It's only corners, throw-ins, and goal kicks." She looked up at the field, where the striker was still being hugged near the corner flag, and tried to rebuild the game in her head with the rule turned right side up. Every goal she'd ever watched, every time she'd hissed at a player for standing lazy and far forward, recalibrated at once.

"Your uncle's going to fight you on this," Tala said, delighted.

"Good," Paige said, though her stomach did something small and complicated, because she had never once corrected him on anything, not the time he'd sworn the earth's seasons were caused by distance from the sun, not the time he'd insisted her mother's car burned premium. She had always acceded, nodded, let it pass, and she was aware, sitting there with the rulebook warm in her hand, that the habit had a cost she'd never bothered to count.

Below them, Klara had abandoned the snack table mid-transaction and climbed the bleachers two at a time, clutching the cash box. "Did we score? I heard the goal but I was making change. Was it a good one?"

"Corner kick, near post, everyone up in arms about offside," Tala said. "Except you can't be offside from a corner, so everyone's wrong and the goal stands and Paige is about to ruin her uncle's whole afternoon."

"That's not what I said," Paige said, but it was close enough to what she'd meant that she didn't argue.

Her uncle had turned around at the sound of his name. "What's that?"

Paige stood up. The wind came off the treeline again and carried a smell of rain that hadn't arrived yet. "There's no offside from a corner," she said, and her voice came out steadier than she expected. "He can stand wherever he wants. It's not an offence just to be there, only if he's involved in the play, and from a corner it doesn't apply at all. Also not from a throw-in or a goal kick."

Her uncle stared at her for a long moment, mouth open, finger still half raised toward the field as though he'd forgotten it was there. Down on the pitch, Mr. Wardak blew his whistle for the restart, and the striker, still grinning, ran back through the boreal light toward the halfway line, entirely innocent of everything he'd been accused of.

"Where did you read that?" her uncle said.

"Right here," Paige said, and held out the phone.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: At the same interest rate, a longer loan term lowers the monthly payment but increases the total interest paid over the life of the loan.
story:
The spreadsheet on Charles's screen had reached the stage where the numbers stopped meaning anything and simply mesmerized him, red cells stacked on blue cells, interest columns lengthening like shadows toward evening. It was past ten on a Tuesday, and his father wanted an answer by morning, because the dealership would only hold the financing offer until Friday. The car was a four-year-old hatchback, silver, twelve thousand dollars, and Charles had spent the evening in the kitchen doorway watching his father sign nothing yet, tapping the pen against the table instead.

He remembered the saleswoman sliding two sheets across the desk that afternoon. On the first, the loan ran three years at a payment of three hundred and eighty dollars. On the second, the same rate, the same car, but seven years, and the monthly figure dropped to two hundred and fifteen. His father's shoulders had come down an inch, the way they did whenever money loosened its grip, and the saleswoman had said the word "affordable" twice, which should have warned them both.

Charles opened the calculator tab again. He typed the payment amounts, multiplied by the months, and the totals arrived without ceremony. Three years: thirteen thousand six hundred and eighty dollars. Seven years: eighteen thousand sixty. Same rate, same car, five thousand dollars apart. He sat back and heard the fridge cycling in the kitchen, his mother's television murmuring below it, the whole house running on its quiet budget of sound.

He called Mahmoud, who picked up on the second ring with his own screen already glowing behind his voice. "Tell me you're not doing homework at ten," Mahmoud said. "It's not homework. My dad's buying the car and they offered him a longer loan to lower the payment. I ran it. The payment goes down but the total interest goes up, a lot. Five grand over the whole loan." There was a pause, then the clatter of Mahmoud typing. "That's actually just how it works, man. Stretch the term, the months pile up." Charles wrote the totals on the back of a water bill so his father wouldn't have to take his word against a saleswoman's.

He kept thinking about the summer before, when his father had replaced the dying water heater on a store credit card and had paid for it, by Charles's later arithmetic, roughly twice over. Not because his father was profligate; there was nothing reckless about him, only tired, and the tiredness was what the offers were engineered to find. Charles had half a politics elective's worth of language for this, something Mr. Ortiz had said in the spring while the class argued about who should regulate banks, about whether we lived, quote, in a technocracy where the numbers know better than we do. At the time Charles had thought it was just a word to fill a whiteboard. Now the whiteboard was his kitchen table and the technocrats were a financing department three towns away, and the knowing better had come down to one kid with a laptop and a water bill.

He walked across the hall to show his father the numbers. His father read the page slowly, twice, the way he read anything that owed him money. "So the lower payment costs more," he said. "That's a dirty trick." "It's not a trick exactly," Charles said, and then stopped, because he wasn't sure it wasn't. "It's just true. Same rate, longer term, more interest total. They told us the payment and not the price." His father set the page down and looked at it as if it might change its mind.

Earlier that evening, before any of this, Charles had opened his own savings account statement, the one holding his wages from two summers of bagging groceries, and noticed the line marked interest: small, patient, sixty-one cents in March. He had never really looked at it before. It was the same principle, turned in the opposite direction, money sitting still and quietly gathering instead of money owed and quietly growing heavier. He didn't mention it to his father, but he thought of Mahmoud's college fund and his own empty one and the two years between him and whatever came next, and how the same arithmetic that made a loan longer made a saver larger, and how nobody had ever put those two facts side by side for him until tonight.

"We could do the three years," his father said. "It's tight but the overtime picks up in spring." He didn't sign anything. He took the water bill with the figures into the living room and turned on the lamp, and Charles went back to his room and left his door open, listening to the pages turn down the hall, and in his savings account, somewhere, sixty-one cents sat earning its sixty-one cents' worth.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: In standard notation, vertical bar lines divide the staff into bars, also called measures, and a final double bar line with one thick line marks the end of a piece.
story:
Kyle had counted the bar lines four times, and four times he came up with fifteen.

The music room smelled like valve oil and the radiator's dry heat, and outside the window the lacrosse team was running laps in the cold. Ms. Reyes had left the chord chart on the board, D minor to B flat to F to C, and under it her instructions in green marker: sixteen bars, notated, with a chord change every two bars, due before the weekend. Kyle sat at the piano with his staff paper in front of him, pencil hovering, the melody complete in his head and somehow wrong on the page.

He had learned the notes from Adelaide, mostly, who had taken piano since she was six and treated theory the way other people treated breathing. She sat two seats away now, headphones around her neck, copying something into her binder with the calm of someone who had never argued with a piece of paper in her life. Kyle had always gone the other way. He played by ear, he made things up, he looped four chords on his phone until his mother knocked on the door. Notation felt like a language he had been locked out of, a whole system that enfranchised anyone who could read it and left him guessing at doors.

"Adelaide," he said. "Can I ask you something that's going to sound stupid?"

"That's how all your questions start."

"I finished the melody. I can play it for you right now, all of it. But when I count it on the page, I get fifteen bars, and it's supposed to be sixteen." He slid the paper across the piano bench. "I've counted the vertical lines, like, four times."

Adelaide put down her pen. She looked at the staff, then at him, and he could see her deciding not to make the joke she usually made. "Count them out loud," she said. "Point at each one."

He pointed. The bar lines ran down through the five lines of the staff, thin and evenly spaced, and he touched each one with his pencil tip. At the end was the double line she had shown him, two lines, the second one thick. "Fifteen lines," he said. "Between them."

"Okay," Adelaide said. "But the last one isn't a bar line. That's the final double bar. It just marks where the piece ends."

Kyle stared at it. "So I don't count it."

"You don't count it. The bar lines divide up the measures. Bars, measures, same thing." She said it lightly, the way she said most things, and turned back to her binder.

He counted again, pencil touching each thin line. Fifteen spaces between sixteen lines meant fifteen bars, and he needed one more, and it was like a floor had shifted under him by an inch. All afternoon he had assumed the page was wrong and his ear was right, that the notation was a recalcitrant bureaucratic form his music was being forced to fill out. But the page was right. His melody was fifteen bars. Somewhere in the second phrase he had let a held note stand where two chords should have passed underneath it, and his ear had smoothed it over because smoothing things over was what his ear did.

He played it through, softly, watching Mathew glance up from the drum pad in the corner. The last phrase hung there, unfinished, landing a bar early. It didn't sound bad. That was the problem. It sounded like a choice, an intentional brevity, and if he left it no one would ever know it was an accident except him.

"So you're a bar short," Mathew said, tapping a soft flam on the pad. "Just repeat the last two chords."

"That's the cheap fix." Kyle played the ending again, then a version where the melody climbed an octave over the final C chord, then a version where it dropped and stopped early, letting the chord ring out alone in the sixteenth bar. Both were honest. Both felt like different pieces.

He thought about what his father said about his grandfather's workshop, how the old man had measured twice and cut once and never trusted a confident hand over a careful one. Kyle had always heard that as a lecture about caution. Now it sounded more like respect, the idea that a form, even a rigid one, was a way of checking yourself against something outside your own head. The notation hadn't fought him. It had caught him.

"Which one?" he asked Adelaide, playing both endings.

She listened with her eyes half closed. "The second one. Where it goes quiet."

"But it might just sound good because it's new."

"Everything sounds good because it's new for about an hour," she said. "Then it's just your song."

Kyle erased nothing. In the sixteenth bar he wrote the final double bar, thin line then thick, and pressed hard enough with the pencil that the thick line came out almost black. He couldn't say yet whether the quiet ending was the true one or only the easier one, and he decided that was a question the melody could hold for now. He slid the paper across to Adelaide. "Count the bars," he said. "I'm not doing it again."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: A blind spot is an area around a car the driver cannot see from the seat, even with mirrors, which is why drivers turn their heads to check before changing lanes.
story:
The driveway was long enough for exactly one mistake at a time, which Ella suspected was why her mother had chosen it. Mr. Haddad, the neighbour whose old sedan sat shaded under the maple, had agreed to supervise her first lesson on the grounds that his insurance was already ruined and a sixteen-year-old could hardly make it worse. Ashwin sat in the back seat because he had failed his own test in June and claimed he wanted to watch her repeat his errors "for scientific purposes," by which he meant entertainment.

"Feet first," Mr. Haddad said. "Then key. Then we discuss what you intend to do, before you do it, at a speed I can interrupt."

Ella adjusted the mirror until it framed the mailbox at the end of the driveway, as if the mailbox were the horizon of her new enfranchised life, licensed to go where the bus did not. Ashwin leaned forward between the seats. "Mirror looks good," he said. "You trust mirrors, right?"

"I trust mirrors," Ella said, and put the car in reverse.

They made it down the driveway without casualties, and then, at Mr. Haddad's direction, out onto the quiet crescent, where the lesson graduated from parking lot liturgy to actual motion. Fifteen kilometers an hour felt like flight. Twenty felt like a hedonistic excess she would pay for later. At the stop sign Mr. Haddad said, "Right turn, signal, check, go," and she did all three in an order he did not entirely approve of.

"The checking," he said. "Do the checking with more conviction."

She turned again, and again, and by the fourth lap of the crescent she had a rhythm: signal, glance at the mirror, drift. Ashwin had his phone half-raised, narrating in a low documentary voice, "Here we observe the learner in her natural habitat, overconfident after four successful turns."

"Shut up, Ashwin."

"I'm providing logos. Evidence. Four turns, zero deaths. Statistically you're immortal."

At the mouth of the crescent, Mr. Haddad told her to pull out onto the collector road, get up to fifty, and merge left at the light. The collector road was empty in the way of roads at ten on a Saturday, so empty that Ella stopped treating it as a road at all and started treating it as an extension of the driveway. She signaled. She looked in the mirror and saw nothing behind her but a stretch of pale asphalt. She began to move left.

"Hold," Mr. Haddad said, one hand rising off his knee, not grabbing the wheel, which somehow was worse than if he had.

There was a grey car beside her. It had been beside her the whole time, close enough that she could see the driver's elbow out the window, and the mirror had shown her none of it. The grey car honked, a short irritated syllable, and slid past and away. Ella's hands were still at ten and two. She had not turned her head. She had trusted the mirror the way she trusted a calculator: completely, and in every case where the case was wrong.

"Back into the right lane," Mr. Haddad said. "Slowly. Then pull over by the mailbox store, whenever you're ready, and take a breath that isn't a performance."

She pulled over. In the back seat Ashwin had gone quiet, which was its own kind of data. Ella looked at the side mirror, then turned her whole head and looked at the empty air beside the car, the space she had not checked.

"That," Ashwin said finally, "was a blind spot. An area around the car you can't see from the seat. Even with mirrors."

"I gathered."

"That's why you turn your head before you change lanes. Like, actually turn it. Bree's brother failed for that."

"I know, Ashwin."

"Your mirror was perfect. That's the evil part."

Ella sat with her hands on the wheel and considered, in the flat fluorescent way of someone recalculating, that her father's version of this lesson had been entirely different: check everything twice, trust no instrument, assume you are wrong. Her mother's version had been closer to Mr. Haddad's, which was no version at all, just repetition until the body believed. She had assumed she belonged to one school or the other. Sitting in the pulled-over car she understood, without being able to say it out loud yet, that the mirror was good and the mirror was not enough, and that both of those things were true at once, and that she would have to turn her head every single time anyway, forever, without ever being certain the turn would reveal something. What she could not figure out was whether the habit was wisdom or just a fence you built because the field was too big to watch.

"Mr. Haddad," she said. "Can we do the merge again?"

"We can do the merge forty more times," he said, checking his own mirror, and then, deliberately, over his shoulder. "Signal first."

She signaled, looked in the mirror where the road lay empty and obedient, and then turned her head.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: Mozart's works are identified by K numbers from the catalogue compiled by Ludwig von Köchel, first published in 1862.
story:
The programme had cost four pounds and Charlotte had already folded it into quarters, which made the small print even harder to read. K. 331, it said, after Piano Sonata No. 11 in A major. She squinted at it under the dimming lights of the concert hall, feeling that the letters were a kind of password she had failed to collect.

"What's the K for?" she whispered to Nour, two seats along.

Nour leaned over, sardonic as ever. "You're doing Mozart for your project and you don't know that?"

"I'm doing the sonata form. The form. First theme, second theme, development, recapitulation. Nobody said anything about letters."

Irene, on Charlotte's other side, plucked the folded programme from her lap and smoothed it against her knee. "It's Köchel," she said. "Mozart's works are identified by K numbers from the catalogue compiled by Ludwig von Köchel, first published in 1862."

"See, Irene knows things," Nour said.

"Irene reads the backs of programmes," Charlotte said, but she said it quietly, because the pianist was already crossing the stage, and because the fact had settled somewhere in her with unexpected weight. A man in the 1860s, a century after Mozart died, had counted and ordered everything, and now the music carried his initials like a second name. She thought of her own notebook at home, its pages gridded into exposition and development and recapitulation, sections boxed and labelled with the confidence of someone who had not yet had to listen.

The first movement was not even the one she was analysing. Mr. Balogun had set the class on the third movement, the one with the famous variation tune, but he had told them they could not understand a set of variations until they understood what it varied from. So she had spent two weeks with the first movement, marking its themes in coloured pencil, and now she was here to hear it live, and the pianist had chosen to begin with the Andante grazioso anyway, which was the first movement, which meant she was lucky, or prepared, or both.

She opened the programme against her knee and tried to follow her own markings. First theme in the opening bars: she had bracketed it in blue. It arrived, precise and small, and she felt the small satisfaction of a map agreeing with the road. Then the transition, which she had marked in pencil because she was never sure where the first theme ended and the second began, whether the passage that shifted toward the dominant was still the first theme becoming something else or already the new one. On paper she had drawn a line. In the hall, the line refused to hold still.

The second theme came in, singing, and she noticed that the pianist leaned back slightly for it, letting it widen. So he heard the boundary too. Or he heard something else that made him move, and she was reading her own map onto his shoulders. She wrote in the margin of the programme, "moved at 2nd theme," and then, honestly, after it, "or before?"

By the development she had stopped writing. The themes broke apart and recombined, and she recognised fragments the way you recognise a friend's laugh in another room. This, at least, was unambiguous; the development eviscerated the material with total courtesy, dismantling her tidy blue brackets and then handing them back, and when the first theme returned near the end, whole and unruffled, she felt the odd relief of the recapitulation, as though the music had been holding its breath for two pages. That was the point of the form, she supposed. Or one point. She was less sure than she had been two weeks ago, which her mother said was what learning looked like, though her mother said that about most things.

At the interval they stood in the crush at the back of the hall. Mr. Balogun was there too, holding a cup of water, and Nour steered them toward him with the frankness of someone who had nothing to lose.

"Sir, Charlotte doesn't know what K means."

"I do now," Charlotte said. "Irene told me. Köchel, 1862." She found she wanted to say it back correctly, to own the fact rather than be caught without it. "It's strange, though. The numbers aren't even the order he wrote them in."

"Catalogues are their own kind of argument," Mr. Balogun said, and sipped his water, and offered nothing further, which was his way of making you do the next part yourself.

She stood there holding the folded programme, thinking that she had two systems in her hands and they did not match. Köchel had counted the works and given each one a number, an orderly encumbrance carried by every sonata forever, and that order was one way of knowing Mozart. Her coloured brackets were another way, and hers kept slipping, the exposition refusing to break cleanly where the textbook said it should. Maybe the form was less a box than a habit the music had, mostly, with exceptions she was supposed to notice rather than repair. She could write that in her project and let Mr. Balogun decide whether honesty counted as analysis.

The bell rang for the second half. The crowd began to move back toward the doors, and Irene pushed the programme into Charlotte's hand, smoothed flat again, creases and all.

"Keep the pencil out," Irene said. "The third movement's next."

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: The 2018 Gender Shades study by Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru found commercial facial analysis systems had error rates up to 34.7 percent for darker-skinned women but under 1 percent for lighter-skinned men.
story:
The bus idled in front of the Meridian building while Ms. Wong counted heads for the third time, and Tristan stood at the back of the line with his lanyard already on, because he wanted, more than anything this semester, to be offered the summer internship they kept mentioning in the assembly slides. He had written the application essay twice. The second draft was the honest one, about wanting to build things people actually used, and he had it saved on his phone like something fragile.

Inside, the lobby was glass and pale wood, and a demo station near the coffee bar showed off the company's new photo app. A young engineer with a tablet invited students to stand in front of a camera and watch the software sort them into a gallery, tag their faces, group them by who appeared most often. Jaxson went first, grinning, and the app found him instantly, framed his face in a neat green box, and labeled him in the corner of the screen.

Jane went second. The box flickered around her and vanished. The engineer tapped the tablet, adjusted a light, asked her to step closer, and the box came back for a half second before dissolving again while Jaxson's photo sat beside hers, already tagged, already sorted. "Try smiling," the engineer said, which Tristan felt in his own face before he understood why. Jane smiled. The software declined to know her.

The engineer moved them along, apologetic and brisk, and Tristan hung back pretending to read a poster about pipeline architecture. He had read something about this, months ago, at two in the morning when he should have been asleep. He found the tab still open in his browser, buried under homework. Jane came and stood next to him, arms folded, and he angled the screen toward her without commentary, the way you hand someone evidence rather than a lecture.

"There was this study," Jane said, reading. "Gender Shades. 2018. Joy Buolamwemi, no, Buolamwini, and Timnit Gebru." Her finger moved down the page. "Commercial facial analysis systems had error rates up to 34.7 percent for darker-skinned women. Under 1 percent for lighter-skinned men." She said it flatly, like a score she had expected. "So Jaxson's under one percent and I'm up to thirty-four point seven." She looked at the poster, then at him. "It's not the lighting."

Tristan wanted to argue, and the wanting itself embarrassed him, because he recognized its shape: the reflex to defend the system he hoped would hire him. In his essay he had written that technology was neutral, that tools only did what their makers intended, and reading that sentence now, in his memory, felt like discovering a crack in something he had built. The logic had seemed airtight, a tidy syllogism: tools serve intentions; intentions can be good; therefore tools can be good. He had not accounted for the possibility that the tools came from somewhere, that they were trained on something, that a dataset could carry a bias in like a dye in water.

The tour moved on to a floor of desks where people watched monitors filled with other people, footage from the company's retail analytics product, anonymized blurs walking store aisles while algorithms counted them. Their guide, a man in a fleece vest, said the word "insights" four times in one minute. Jaxson asked whether the counting software had the same trouble with faces that the photo app did, and the guide said that the retail product didn't identify individuals, only patterns, which seemed to Tristan like a distinction that depended on who was doing the distinguishing. The whole floor smelled like carpet and ambition, and every gain he had imagined for himself, the internship, the badge, the building, sat now next to a cost he hadn't priced.

At the end, in a conference room with sandwiches, Ms. Wong had them go around and say one thing that surprised them. When it was Tristan's turn, he had planned to say something safe about the server room, but he heard himself say, "The demo didn't recognize Jane. It recognized Jaxson right away." The recruiter at the far end of the table stopped writing. The silence had a texture to it, faintly electric, an embryonic accountability that might become something or might be smoothed over by the next sentence, and Tristan understood he had probably, in a small quiet way, destabilized his own application.

The recruiter said, "That's a known issue we're working on," and a few students nodded, and Jaxson said nothing, and Jane ate her sandwich. On the bus home she sat next to Tristan and looked out the window at the building shrinking behind them. "You didn't have to say it," she said. He shrugged, not sure whether he had done something brave or only something loud. "You should still apply," Jane said. "Fix it from the inside, isn't that the whole point?" Tristan pulled out his phone, opened the essay, and deleted the sentence about tools being neutral. Then he sat there a while with the cursor blinking, not yet sure what should go in its place, while the highway noise filled in around them and Jane watched the guardrails slide past.

"Thirty-four point seven," she said, mostly to the window. "Under one."

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: A 2019 study led by Ziad Obermeyer found a widely used US health-care algorithm underestimated Black patients' needs because it used past medical spending as a stand-in for how sick patients were.
story:
Victoria had been accepted to three colleges and harassed by eleven of their alumni fundraising algorithms, so her position on technology was complicated before she opened the laptop that evening. She sat at the desk in her room with the window cracked because the radiator clanked like it was settling a grudge, and typed "health algorithm bias" into the search bar for the fourth time, because her scholarship essay was due Friday and she still had nothing but a memory.

The memory was from a field trip in October, before anyone knew she would be going anywhere. Their computer science class had toured a company that built software for hospitals, all glass walls and badges that beeped, and during the Q and A Angelina had raised her hand and asked how an engineer knows what a data label really measures. The engineer had paused, the way people pause when the honest answer is longer than the polite one, and said that was the best question of the day, which was not an answer at all. Mr. Kaya had written something in his notebook. Victoria had written "label" in hers and underlined it twice for no reason she could defend.

Kierra, sprawled on the bed behind her with her phone held above her face, said, "You're doing the essay again."

"I'm doing the essay finally."

"Because I found the thing." Kierra sat up in the way of someone about to make a presentation. She read off her phone that in 2019 a study led by Ziad Obermeyer looked at a health-care algorithm used all over the US, and it found the algorithm underestimated how sick Black patients were. "Because it used how much they'd spent on care as a stand-in for how sick they were."

Victoria turned around in the chair. "Meaning less money spent, the algorithm reads that as less sick."

"That's what it says. Whether that's what it means is your essay." Kierra flopped back down, then popped up again. "Also, put my name on it. Like a thank-you. Or a co-author line."

"You sent me a link."

"Collaboration has degrees."

Victoria pulled the study up herself and read it twice, slowly, the way she read things she intended to argue with. Less spending read as less need, and so less need meant less help, and none of it required anyone to be malevolent, which was the part that kept snagging her. She had grown up on movies where the machine was evil and the problem was a villain in a hoodie. This was worse in a quieter way: a spreadsheet doing arithmetic, faithfully, on the wrong question. Nobody had to stigmatize anybody. The data did it for them, politely, at scale.

She started drafting. She wrote that people treated algorithms like arbitration, a neutral judge weighing evidence, but a judge could only weigh what it was handed, and what it had been handed was spending. She wrote that her grandmother had put off a hip replacement for two years because of the bills, and she caught herself and deleted it, then put it back, because it was true and because true was the point. She was still deciding between the two versions, honest and cleaner, when Kierra leaned over her shoulder.

"It's good," Kierra said. "It's not going to win anything with that ending, though. Judges like a fix. Say what you'd change."

"I don't know what I'd change."

"Say that anyway but in a nicer font."

Victoria looked at the screen. Somewhere under the study was the company they had visited, or one like it, all glass walls, and somewhere under that were the labels Angelina had asked about, and under that, maybe, was the question of whether you could ever really know what a number was standing in for. She thought you probably couldn't, not all the way, and that you had to build things anyway, and that both of those could be true at once, though she couldn't yet say how to write that sentence so it didn't sound like a shrug.

She typed the grandmother paragraph back in, then sat with her hands off the keys. The radiator clanked. Kierra held out her phone, showing a job application for a café that wanted her to record a two-minute video answering why she loved coffee, and said, "Real quick, before your brain eats itself. Do I say I love coffee?"

"Do you love coffee?"

"I love having money."

Victoria typed one more line, then swiveled the chair around. "Say you love the smell. Nobody can fact-check the smell."

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: Steelmanning is the practice of restating an opposing argument in its strongest form, even stronger than the other person put it, before responding to it.
story:
The debate team met on Tuesdays in the portable classroom behind the gym, and Maria arrived early because she wanted the seat by the window. Micaela was already there, spreading index cards across two desks, and Calista stood at the whiteboard drawing arrows between phrases like "school policy" and "surveillance." The resolution this month was whether their school should sell student browsing data to education software companies in exchange for free tablets. Ms. Campbell had chosen it, she said, because it was an argument nobody could feel clean about.

Maria had drawn the affirmative by lot, which meant she had to defend the sale. She'd spent three nights drafting and every draft collapsed the same way: if the students consent, then the exchange is voluntary, and if it's voluntary, it isn't exploitation, but the consent came from a district that had already decided, so the conditional was rigged from the first letter. She'd written that sentence in the margin of her notes, and Micaela had read it upside down and asked whether she was arguing or auditing herself. Metacognition, Calista had said from the whiteboard, thinking about your thinking, like a mirror facing a mirror. She'd said it as an accusation.

The practice round began after the bell for late buses. Micaela argued the negative, and she argued it badly on purpose, Maria realized only later. If we sell the data, she said, then the companies will just commodify everything about us, our searches, our hesitations, the seconds we pause on a question, until students become products walking around in uniform polos. Maria stood to respond and heard herself start with the weak version: companies already track us anyway, so we might as well get tablets out of it. Micaela yawned, openly, and the yawn was the whole point.

"You're attacking the worst thing I said," Micaela said, "not the best thing."

Ms. Campbell, sorting papers at her desk, said nothing, but she'd stopped sorting.

Calista turned around from the board. "There's a word for the opposite. You restate my argument so it's stronger than I made it, then you answer that. It's called steelmanning." She said it fast, the way she said things she'd learned the night before and wanted everyone to know she'd learned first. Maria understood, watching Micaela's flat expression, that Calista's want this afternoon wasn't winning the debate; it was being the person who knew the word.

So Maria tried it. She stood with her hands flat on the desk and restated the negative: if browsing data reveals how a student thinks, and that data belongs to a company rather than to the student, then the school has traded away something the student can't repurchase, because you cannot buy back a record of your own hesitation once it has informed an algorithm. The pause data. The seconds on a question. She said it better than Micaela had, and she felt the room tilt, because now she was arguing against a version of the case that she partly believed. Her prepared rebuttals, the consent chain, the voluntary exchange, looked thin against it. Consent given under a district mandate, she said slowly, resembles consent the way a fire drill resembles a fire.

Micaela had stopped yawning. "That's my argument," she said. "Better than mine."

"And it still loses," Maria said, "or I can't yet see how it doesn't lose to something. Maybe to the condition that the data is aggregated, not individual. But I don't know if aggregation fixes it or just hides it." She sat down without a closing line, which was against every rule of the format, and Ms. Campbell marked something on her clipboard, and Maria couldn't tell from her jaundiced view of the score sheet whether the mark was good.

Calista erased her arrows and started drawing new ones, ones that led from "strongest opposing case" to "conditional concessions," and she talked while she drew, about how you could nest an if inside an if, consent holds if the process is fair, the process is fair if the district has no stake, the district has a stake, therefore. Maria watched the marker squeak and thought about her father, who had said at dinner that she could keep the car only if she was home by eleven, and who had reasons she'd never once tried to state in their strongest form: insurance, the county road after dark, the two boys who'd gone off the bridge curve in November. She had always answered the weakest version of him, the version that said because I said so.

She said none of this aloud. Instead she copied Calista's diagram into her notebook, including the nested conditionals, and under the word steelman she wrote, in small letters, tonight, dinner. Micaela leaned over and read it, and raised her eyebrows, and Maria shook her head once, meaning later, meaning maybe, meaning I don't know yet what I'll say to him, only that I'll say his side first.

On the way out, Calista held the door and said, "You know I was the one who brought it up." Maria zipped her bag and looked at the parking lot, where the late buses were idling in a row, one of them hers. "I know," she said. "That's why I wrote it down before the board got erased."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During China's Qingming Festival, which falls on April 4, 5 or 6, families visit their ancestors' graves to sweep and clean them and leave offerings of food.
story:
The house still smelled of his grandfather's tea, though it had been three months since the funeral, and Edouard stood in the kitchen doorway of the little bungalow feeling like an intruder in his own inheritance. His grandmother was at the table with a cardboard box, laying out objects in rows: a whisk broom with split bristles, a tin of shortbread, a roll of paper towels, three oranges. She did not look up when he came in.

"There you are," she said. "Help me with the box."

He sat across from her and turned the broom over in his hands. It was cheap, the kind sold at a dollar store, and he could not imagine what it was for, since his grandfather had owned a proper push broom that still leaned in the garage. "Whose is this?"

"Mine now. It was his, before." She took it back gently, the way she handled things that had been his, and set it with the oranges. "It's almost the fifth," she added, as if that settled everything. It settled nothing for Edouard. The fifth of April meant nothing to him except that his college deposit was due in two weeks, and that Lynden had already texted twice asking whether he'd decided.

At the cemetery the next morning, the wind moved through the grass in long diurnal shifts, bright then grey, bright then grey, and Edouard carried the box while his grandmother walked ahead of him with a pace that dared him to slow her down. Other families were scattered across the hillside. He noticed them one by one: a woman wiping a headstone with a cloth, children raking leaves from a plot, an old man arranging what looked like a whole meal, bowls and chopsticks, on the flat stone in front of a grave. Edouard stared at that longer than he meant to.

"They leave food," he said.

"They leave food," his grandmother agreed, and knelt at the footpath to brush dried grass off the approach to the plot. "Twice he took me back to Guangzhou to do this for his mother. Both times in April. I thought it was superstition then. I ascribed it to, I don't know, something old in him that America hadn't worn off." She began to sweep the stone itself, short strokes, top to base, and handed him the paper towels.

He cleaned the engraved name while she watched, and he understood, without anyone saying it, that the sweeping was not preparation for something else. It was the thing itself. The dates on the stone were the dates he knew by heart, and the orange he set at the base was an orange, but he placed it the way he had seen the old man do it, centered, stem down, and heard his grandmother exhale behind him.

"He wanted you to know this," she said. "Every spring. April fourth, fifth, or sixth, that's when families come. That's the whole of it, the grave sweeping. He'd have taken you himself." She sat back on her heels. "Last year I told him you were busy. You were. There was the debate tournament, the thing with Hailey, all of it. I said, he's seventeen, next year. That was my call, not yours. I want you to know that."

Edouard thought about the year he had been given back, in a sense, and could not decide whether he had spent it well or merely spent it. He had won the tournament, or at least the regional round, standing in the school's oratory delivering a eulogy for a fictional senator he had invented and pitied more than he had ever pitied his actual grandfather, who was then still alive and waiting for April. He had not known there was an April. That was the part he could not forgive or stop examining: not that he had been busy, but that being busy had felt like a reason.

He swept the stone a second time, though it was already clean. His grandmother ate half a shortbread and left the rest on the paper towel, and they sat in the wind while other families worked their way down the hill, and Edouard took out his phone and typed a message to Lynden and then deleted it, because whatever he had to say about the deposit could wait until tomorrow. When the light shifted grey again his grandmother held out her hand for the box, and he helped her up, and together they walked down past the plot where the old man was now sitting cross-legged beside his offerings, talking steadily to the stone as though the person inside had only to be coaxed into answering.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: US food safety guidance says perishable food should not sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours, or one hour when it is above 90 degrees.
story:
Jasmine counted the bills in her pocket twice before she left the house, because the farmers' market closed at one and dinner depended on what fourteen dollars could do. In the kitchen there were tomatoes going soft on the windowsill, a bag of potatoes, and a mother who had worked the night shift and would sleep until five. That was the shape of the plan: buy what the garden and the pantry couldn't give, cook before her mother woke, have it on the table like an argument for something she hadn't named yet.

The market occupied half the elementary school parking lot, white tents in a ragged line. She went first to Mr. Watanabe's stall, because he sold eggs and soft cheese and kept a small cooler of ice packs he was generous with, and because he was the only vendor who didn't watch her hands when she lingered.

"Two dozen eggs," she said. "And the cheese, if it's not too much."

"It's never too much," Mr. Watanabe said. "You cooking tonight?" He wrapped the cheese in waxed paper, then slid an ice pack alongside it without being asked. "It'll be ninety-two by noon. You keep this with it until you're home."

"An hour, then," she said, mostly to herself, and he nodded like she'd passed some small test.

She had learned the rule in the spring, from a card at the library, when she'd volunteered to run the snack table at Orlando's younger brother's birthday. Perishable food should not sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours, and only one hour once the day went above 90. She'd taped the card inside her notebook then, half embarrassed by it, and now the numbers surfaced the way multiplication did, without asking permission. The ice pack wasn't fussiness; it was arithmetic.

At the far end of the tents she found Orlando stacking his aunt's zucchini into a pyramid nobody would buy in this heat. "You look like somebody with a plan," he said.

"Dinner. For my mom. She doesn't think I can do it without setting off the smoke alarm." She turned a zucchini over, felt the incipient softness at one end, the first surrender of it, and put it back. "That's not really why, though. She thinks I can't finish anything."

"So this is a predicate," Orlando said. "Dinner is the thing the whole argument depends on."

She laughed before she could stop herself. "Did you just use predicate as a noun?"

"It can be one. Look it up." He bagged three firm ones anyway and took only a dollar for them, which she let him do because refusing would have cost them both something.

Walking home, she pulled out her phone. There was a message from Carson, sent that morning, and she read it again under the shade of the school's maples.

 Heard you're cooking. Also my mom says ask your mom about the cookout leftovers, the ones from Saturday still out on your porch table?? She says if it was hot yesterday, most of that's done. Don't be gross about it, J. Call me if you want, I'm around till 4.

Jasmine stood still with the bag of zucchini against her hip. Saturday's cookout. The potato salad, the burger platter, the bowl of her aunt's shrimp. Her mother had left everything out on the porch table when the last guests went, saying the night air would keep it, and then sleeping through Sunday and working Sunday night, and now it was Monday and the platters were probably still there in the sun, and her mother would wake up at five and put the shrimp in the refrigerator out of thrift, out of the reflex that waste was the real sin.

She called Carson from the porch, looking at the table while the phone rang. The potato salad had gone pale at the edges. A wasp worked the rim of the burger platter.

"Tell me what your mom said," Carson said, picking up on the first ring.

"That it sat out all Saturday afternoon and all night and all Sunday. It was above ninety both days."

"Then it's been in the danger zone way past the one hour. The whole two-hour rule is already blown by a day, J. My mom says when it's that hot you get one hour, period."

"One hour," Jasmine repeated. Behind her the screen door opened an inch and stopped, the way it did when her mother was half awake and listening without committing to being there. Jasmine looked at the table, then at the door, then at the table again. She thought of Mr. Watanabe sliding the ice pack in without being asked, and of Orlando calling dinner a predicate, the thing the whole claim rested on, and she understood that the claim rested on this too: throwing out her aunt's shrimp while her mother watched.

"Okay," she said to Carson. "Thanks." She hung up and picked up the shrimp bowl first, because it was the worst of it and the bowl was heavy, and she carried it past the half-open screen door toward the trash cans at the side of the house.

"Jasmine." Her mother's voice, rough with sleep, from somewhere inside. "What are you doing with that?"

"Ask me at dinner," Jasmine said, and kept walking, the bowl tilted against her hip, the ice pack in her market bag already going soft.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Artists commonly keep two versions of their statement: a short one of about 50 to 100 words and a longer one of about 500 to 1,000 words.
story:
Hannah's grandmother's dining table was too large for one girl and a laptop, but Hannah spread her ten canvases across it anyway, smallest to largest, the way a dealer might lay out cards. The house smelled of lavender and old paper, and through the window the garden was recovering from August, half its colours spent. She had promised her art teacher a complete portfolio by Friday, and the portfolio was finished. What she did not have was the statement.

She had written it four times already that morning. The first attempt began, "My work explores themes of memory and impermanence," which she deleted because it sounded like every artist's statement she had ever read aloud in class. The second began with an anecdote about her grandmother's hands. The third was three sentences. The fourth was four pages, and even she had stopped reading it halfway through.

Her phone buzzed against the wood. London, texting from the art supply shop where she worked weekends for what London called "scandalous remuneration," which Hannah understood to mean minimum wage and a discount on gouache. There's a guy here, London wrote. Retired gallery owner. Buying varnish. He's talking about statements. Want me to ask him something?

Hannah typed back, Ask him how long mine should be, then felt embarrassed and added a smiley so it would look like a joke.

Twenty minutes later London sent a photo of a page in the man's notebook. He says most artists keep two versions. A short one, about 50 to 100 words, for wall cards and small things. A long one, 500 to 1,000 words, for applications. He says everybody does it and I should stop looking at him like he's a wizard.

Hannah read the message three times. Two versions. Not because one was better than the other, but because they did different jobs. The short one had to stand beside the art in a room where people were already looking; the long one had to speak for the art in a room where nobody could see it. She sat with that for a while, turning her grandmother's sugar spoon over in her fingers, wondering whether that was a compromise or just honesty about context. Maybe both.

She tried the short version first, out loud, to the room. "I paint the same garden at different hours because my grandmother, who is eighty-four, keeps saying she'll get to the roses tomorrow." Fifty words, give or take. It sounded, she thought, like something a person would actually say, which was either the goal or a sign she was doing it wrong. Her grandmother came in with tea, set down two cups, and looked at the canvases arranged across her table.

"All my garden," she said.

"All your garden," Hannah agreed. "Is that strange?"

Her grandmother considered it, sardonic and unhurried, the way she was about most things Hannah treated as emergencies. "It's my garden. It's your seeing. Those are two different objects, whatever the canvas says." She tapped the largest one, the roses at eleven in the morning, and left the room before Hannah could decide whether she'd been complimented.

The long statement took the rest of the afternoon. Hannah wrote about her grandmother's postponements, about how a garden keeps making the same promise and keeping it differently every year, about the fact that she had painted the roses four times and they were never the same roses. She deleted the sentence about memory and impermanence twice more, both times recognizing it as a costume she put on when she wanted to sound like an artist instead of being one. By five o'clock she had 700 words, which she counted twice, and she thought she understood, at last, why the short version was harder. It was not a summary of the long one. It was a different genre entirely. Compression wasn't the same as abbreviation; a small door still had to open onto the same room.

She was still unsure, though, whether the two statements should sound like the same person. The short one was plain and a little funny. The long one was plainer than she'd expected it to be, but more patient, willing to circle back. Were those two voices, or one voice at two volumes? She couldn't decide, and she couldn't find the retired gallery owner to ask, and London had gone off shift.

Mischa arrived at six with her own portfolio, uninvited, because Mischa believed deadlines were group events. She read Hannah's short statement standing up, in one minute, then sat and read the long one for eleven minutes without speaking, which for Mischa was unprecedented.

"They're both you," Mischa said finally. "That's the weird part. I believed both."

Hannah looked at the pages side by side on the table, one a slip of paper, one a small stack, the same garden behind both of them in the window going blue. She still didn't know if the voices matched on purpose or by accident, and she suspected she wouldn't know until a stranger read them a year from now, in some gallery she couldn't picture yet.

"Help me hang them in order," she said, and began lifting the canvases from the table, smallest first, the evening light catching the wet varnish on the eleven o'clock roses.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Compound interest follows A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), where n is how many times per year interest is added, so more frequent compounding gives a slightly larger total.
story:
Victor had saved four thousand dollars over two summers of bagging groceries, and he had decided, on the bus ride over, that today he would look at the gray hatchback in the second row and not say anything stupid. His mother came with him because he was seventeen and the dealership would not let him test drive alone. The salesman, a tall man with a lanyard, walked them past a truck the color of a littoral sky, all pale blue and chrome, and Victor kept his eyes on the hatchback.

"It's listed at eleven two," the salesman said, and then, almost in the same breath, "but you can drive it for two sixty a month." Victor did the division in his head and came out with something over five years, and the total was more than eleven two. He asked why, and the salesman said, "Interest," the way people say weather. "The money you borrow costs money."

His mother sat down at the little table with the paper coffee cups while the salesman went to the back office to requisition a copy of their insurance card from the finance desk. Victor wandered. The showroom was quiet in the middle of a Tuesday, and through the plate glass he could see the lot like a steppe, flat and enormous, rows of vehicles standing where grass should have been. On the wall behind the finance desk hung a whiteboard with rates, and next to it a sign about the dealership's own savings program for employees, which nobody was reading.

He texted Lea, who worked Saturdays at the credit union near school. "At a dealership. They want me to pay interest. Like a penalty for not having money."

Her reply came while his mother was still filling out the form. "That's one way to look at it. It works both directions, though. Interest you pay on a loan, interest you earn on savings. At the credit union we have two accounts for teens. Mine compounds monthly. The other one compounds yearly. Same rate otherwise."

"What's compounding," he typed, and then deleted it, because he could guess: interest earning interest. He typed instead, "Monthly vs yearly matters?" and she wrote back, "Yeah. More times a year it gets added, the bigger the total ends up. Formula's on the brochure, A equals P times one plus r over n, to the nt. The n is how many times per year. It's not a huge difference. But it's a difference."

He read it twice. It was strange to think of the same force running in both directions, that the number on the whiteboard behind the finance desk and the number on Lea's brochure were the same animal, just facing opposite ways. He pocketed the phone when the salesman returned.

The finance manager was a woman with reading glasses on a chain, and she was kinder than the numbers on her screen. "You've got four thousand," she said, looking at his mother's paperwork, then at Victor. "That's a real down payment. But if you borrow the rest at this rate, over five years, you'll pay more than a thousand extra for the car. That's the honest number. Some people don't want the honest number." She slid a printout across the table, and Victor saw the two columns, what he'd owe each month and what he'd owe altogether, and the second one was the kind of number that followed you.

His mother asked about a shorter loan. The manager recalculated, and the monthly payment climbed while the total sank, and Victor watched the two numbers move against each other like people negotiating in another room. He thought about Lea's message. If he put the four thousand in the account that compounded monthly instead of yearly, it would grow faster, not by much, but in the right direction. If he borrowed seven thousand, it would also grow, in the wrong direction, by more than much. He could wait a year, save another three thousand, borrow less or nothing. A year felt long. The hatchback sat in the second row, gray and patient, and it would be gone by then, and another one exactly like it would be somewhere else.

"We should go," his mother said quietly, and he could tell she had done her own math and was trying not to decide for him. That was the thing he noticed most, in the end. She put her hand flat on the table, not on his shoulder, and waited.

"Can I keep the printout?" Victor asked the finance manager. She said of course, and folded it in half for him, and on the way out he stopped to text Lea: "Monthly. Thank you." The salesman held the door, and Victor's mother asked if he was okay. He said he was, and mostly he was, except for the part of him already turning over how a year of waiting could be worth a thousand dollars, and the other part that wanted the car now, and no way to make those two parts sit still. He looked back once at the lot, all that flat shining metal, and then followed his mother to the bus stop.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Many news stories begin with a dateline naming the city where the story was reported, placed before the first sentence.
story:
The festival had taken over the whole waterfront park, and Gabrielle had promised herself she would do one brave thing before the afternoon ended. She had chosen it weeks ago, in the dull shame of a Sunday afternoon: the news corner, where anyone could take a short article in another language, read it aloud, and summarise it for the small crowd. Her grandmother's language, the one her mother had decided not to pass on, sat on the rack between Japanese and Korean, a thin newspaper from Maputo with a photograph of fishing boats on the front. Gabrielle took it and joined the queue behind a boy struggling through a Spanish piece about football.

She had learned the alphabet last month from a borrowed book, then the ordinary words, then the trickier ones. What she could not learn from a book was the reason her mother had let the language lapse, and this was the part that gnawed at her while she waited. Her grandmother had offered Sunday lessons for years, and Gabrielle had begged off for swim practice, for sleep, for nothing at all. She had come to think of the news corner as a way to expiate some of that, though she knew a three-minute reading was a small payment for four years of closed doors.

Rosa found her in the queue, lanyard swinging, clipboard against her chest. "You're actually doing it," Rosa said. "I put you sixth. I wanted you early, before the judges drift off to the food stalls." Rosa had wanted to run the news corner all spring, had lobbied Ms. Nkosi for the volunteer coordinator role, and had designed the little paper tickets herself. She believed that if the corner went well, Ms. Nkosi would recommend her for the youth council, and the youth council, Rosa was convinced, was the first real rung of everything.

"Sixth is fine," Gabrielle said, but her hands were cold on the newspaper. Ahead of her, a girl read a French article about a bridge and summarised it in careful, flat sentences. The crowd clapped. The crowd would clap for anything, which was somehow worse.

When her turn came, Gabrielle stood at the low podium and unfolded the paper. The article was short, thank God, something about two fishing cooperatives that had signed an agreement after years of quarrelling over waters, an armistice that the writer seemed to doubt would hold. She read haltingly, hearing her own errors, hearing her grandmother's voice correcting her inside her skull, and then she closed the paper and summarised. "It is about fishing villages in Portugal," she said. "Two groups stopped fighting."

A man in the third row raised his hand. He spoke calmly, in an accent close to her grandmother's. "Which city is the story from, my daughter?"

"Lisbon," Gabrielle said, because Lisbon was where Portuguese newspapers came from, as far as she knew.

He shook his head, not unkindly. "Look at the little word before the first sentence. In capital letters."

Rosa watched from the side of the podium, and it was Rosa who felt the drop in her stomach, a heavier drop than the mistake deserved. She had checked the article herself when she filed the papers that morning; she had read the masthead, skimmed the photo caption, and never once looked at the small line of capitals at the top of the text. If Gabrielle had named the wrong country in front of a native speaker, some part of that was Rosa's corner, Rosa's tickets, Rosa's recommendation. She saw Gabrielle's eyes move down the page, saw them stop.

"Oh," Gabrielle said. "Maputo." The capitals sat there plainly, before the first sentence of the story, naming the city where the story had been reported, and she had simply skipped over them as if they were decoration. "It's from Maputo. In Mozambique." The country shifted under her feet. The article was about the littoral towns north of the city, the string of fishing settlements along that coast, and she had dragged them three thousand kilometres across an ocean to a country she had chosen only because it was the one she had heard of.

"Dateline," said Estelle, who had come up from the audience with her phone in her hand, having been silently checking Gabrielle's claims. "They call that the dateline." She said it the way she reported everything, quickly and without ceremony, and Rosa could have kissed her, because now the correction had come from a peer and not from the man, and the moment had stayed soft.

Gabrielle asked whether she could try again. Ms. Nkosi, who had been standing near the ticket table all afternoon with her arms folded, nodded once, so Gabrielle opened the paper and summarised it properly: an agreement between two cooperatives from the Mozambican coast, signed in Maputo, which the reporter covering the story seemed to trust about halfway. Her Portuguese still broke in the same places, but the man in the third row smiled at her, and one or two others clapped, and Rosa wrote something on her clipboard that was not part of any scoring sheet.

Afterward, walking between the stalls with Estelle, Gabrielle turned the mistake over without deciding anything about it. She had wanted, she realised, to feel the language as an inheritance, something that would rise out of her whole if she only knocked on the right door, and instead she had found a craft with small rules she had never been taught, a line of capitals she had walked straight past. Her mother's choice to withhold the language still seemed wrong to her, or at least unfair, but she could no longer pretend that the withholding was the whole reason she didn't know it. She had skipped the Sunday lessons herself, Sundays when her grandmother had waited with tea.

"Will you call your grandmother?" Estelle asked. "Tell her you read a whole article?"

"I'll tell her I read one wrong first," Gabrielle said. "That's the better story."

She bought a pastry at the Mozambican stall, because the man at the griddle had the same accent, and she asked him, in her broken, mended Portuguese, whether the towns in the article were near where he had grown up.

"Not so near," he said. "But the coast is one coast."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
