knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Earth's surface gives off heat as infrared radiation; greenhouse gases absorb much of it and re-emit it in all directions, including back down, which warms the lower atmosphere.
story:
The sand was still warm at seven in the evening, long after the sun had gone low and orange, and Charles kept his sneakers on because of it. In his backpack, folded twice, was the handout Ms. Kapoor had given back to him with one word in red at the top: again. He had forty hours to rebuild the presentation, and the part he'd gotten wrong, apparently, was the first part, the part he'd thought was the easy part.

"You're staring at the ocean like it insulted you," Mischa said, dropping onto the sand beside him with a thermos. Mischa was voluble in the evenings, words coming faster and warmer as the light went down, and Charles had learned not to try to steer him, only to wait.

"It kind of did." Charles pulled out the handout and smoothed the fold. The graph ran across the page, a rising line, jagged like a saw, climbing decade over decade. Below it his own handwriting ran out in a dead end: the gases "reflect heat," he had written, and Ms. Kapoor had circled reflect twice.

Coralie came back from the waterline with her shoes in one hand and her phone in the other. "Look at this thing my cousin lent me," she said. She turned the screen toward them: a thermal camera app, the world rendered in bruised purples and a hard white where the sun still struck the wet sand. "Watch." She held her palm close above the dry sand without touching it, and on the screen a yellow bloom opened under her hand, spreading like something poured.

"That's the sand's heat," she said. "It's giving it off right now. You can feel it on your ankles."

Charles took the phone. On the screen the whole beach glowed faintly, and above it the sky showed almost black. "So why doesn't it all just go up," he said slowly, "out to space? It's rising off the ground right now. The sky's black. It should escape."

Mischa started an answer about cold air and convection, something he'd half absorbed from a documentary, and Charles let him run while he watched the yellow bloom under his own hand, held a foot above the sand now, dimmer but still there. The heat reached upward. Something in the air, he thought, was meeting it.

"It's in the air," he said, mostly to himself, and Mischa stopped mid-sentence, which almost never happened. "The gases in the air. They take the heat in. The heat the ground gives off." He turned the phone so Coralie could see the sky's black ceiling again. "And then they send it back out. In every direction." He pointed down at the sand, then up, then sideways. "Every direction. Including back down."

"Down at us," Coralie said.

"Down at us. That's why the air near the ground is warmer." He said it and then checked himself, because he'd been wrong before with more confidence than this. "I think that's why. That's the thing I wrote wrong. I said they bounce it, like a mirror. It's not a mirror. It's more like the gas swallows it and then spits it out every which way, and some of what gets spat out comes back down."

Mischa lay back on the sand, which was itself radiating, and laughed at the ceiling. "So we're standing in the spit."

"That's a travesty of what I said," Charles said, but he was laughing too, and the laughing loosened something. He looked at the handout again, at the saw-toothed climb of the line. The graph and the glowing beach were not two subjects, he understood suddenly, they were one subject. The line was the count of the gases in the air, and the gases were the reason the yellow bloom under Coralie's hand would keep finding its way back down to her ankles. Ms. Kapoor would want him to say which part stayed uncertain, so he rehearsed it: he could say what the gases did, and he could say the line had gone up over the last century, and he could not yet say, in any clean sentence, how much of the one followed from the other. He would have to stand there on Tuesday and admit the seam.

Coralie reclaimed her phone and held it up to film the three of them against the violet water, and on the little screen they appeared as three pale fires, flickering above a beach that glowed like a coal.

"Say the thing again," she said. "For the video. The every-direction part."

Charles held out his hand toward the warm sand, palm down, like a man swearing an oath. "It comes back down," he said. "Some of it comes back down."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The yellow first-down line shown on televised American football is computer-drawn; it was first broadcast on ESPN on September 27, 1998, by a company called Sportvision.
story:
The last Sunday of September, Kyle's grandfather declared that everyone would watch the game at his house, and nobody had argued, because nobody argued with him about football. The den smelled of cedar and onion dip, and the old recliner had been reserved since morning by a folded blanket, a territorial claim everyone respected. Kyle sat on the floor with his back against the couch, Mackenzie beside him with her boots tucked under her, Belle on the armrest, and the youngest cousin, a boy of seven who followed Kyle everywhere, wedged in between them like a comma.

The argument started in the second quarter, when the yellow line appeared across the field and the cousin said, matter-of-factly, "That's the paint they put down for first down." Kyle laughed before he could stop himself, and his grandfather, without turning from the screen, said, "He's right, you know. Grounds crew marks it before the play." Kyle felt the room divide quietly, Mackenzie smirking at him, Belle looking studiously neutral, and he understood that he was about to have this fight whether he wanted it or not.

He tried the obvious first. "Grandpa, the players run over it. It doesn't smudge. It moves every first down." His grandfather said cameras could do wonderful things, which was not agreement but retreat, and retreat from him was a kind of victory that Kyle distrusted. He cogitated on the problem through the next series of downs, because there was a right answer here somewhere and he did not yet have it; he only had the observation, and observations without evidence persuaded no one, least of all a man who had watched games since before Kyle's father was born.

What Kyle needed was the history, so he pulled out his phone and typed while the crowd on television roared at nothing in particular. The facts arrived in fragments and then in order. The line was computer-drawn, laid onto the broadcast image, not onto the grass. It had first appeared on ESPN on September 27, 1998. He looked at his grandfather, who was sixty-eight years old, and did a small arithmetic he didn't like the answer to: the yellow line had existed for more than half of his grandfather's life. There had been a time, a long time, when his grandfather had watched without it, and had never noticed the day it arrived.

From the couch, Belle had been watching Kyle's face change, and she could tell the moment he found what he was looking for, because his thumbs stopped and his shoulders settled, the way they did when he finished a proof in geometry. She had known him since eighth grade and knew the difference between his smug look and his careful one; this was the careful one, and it made her curious what he would do with it, since he was perfectly capable of winning an argument in a way that left everyone worse off.

Kyle lowered the phone. "It's not paint," he said. "It's drawn by computer, onto the broadcast. First time was ESPN, September 27, 1998." His grandfather snorted. "Computers. Then who drew it, some kind of ideologue in a back room?" Kyle shook his head and found the name. "A company did it. It was called Sportvision." The cousin repeated the word, Sportvision, like a spell, and Mackenzie said, "Ninety-eight, so you were forty-four," which was the sentence that changed the room.

His grandfather was quiet for a long moment, and Kyle watched him take it in, the way the man's jaw worked as though chewing something tough. Kyle understood, then, that he had won the fact and lost something else, because his grandfather had not been lying or being stubborn; he had been remembering a field he thought he knew, and the yellow line had moved in like a tenant who never introduced himself. Kyle had corrected him in front of a seven-year-old who idolized them both, and the correction was true, and truth delivered in front of witnesses still had a cost. Belle saw Kyle see it, and she reached over and stole a chip from his plate, which was her way of saying the world was still fine.

For a while nobody spoke, and the game went on, and the yellow line glowed at the ten, then the thirty-five, faithful and weightless. In the fourth quarter, his grandfather lifted the cousin onto his lap and said, to the boy and not to Kyle, "Tell you a secret. When I was your age, there wasn't any line at all. You had to guess where they had to get to." The cousin looked at the screen as though it had turned malevolent, hiding things from old people, and asked, "Then how did you know?" His grandfather smiled at the television, and Kyle, listening from the floor, waited for an answer that did not come.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The US Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act of 1996 gives food donors limited protection from liability, which encourages stores and restaurants to donate surplus food.
story:
Annabelle signed in at the front desk of the public library at eight-forty on a Saturday morning, though the library itself would not open for another twenty minutes. In the meeting room beyond the returns counter, folding tables had been pushed together under a banner that read Monthly Food Bank Distribution, and a man in a library staff polo was already carrying boxes from the loading door. She had volunteered because her college application was finished and her summer had settled into a turbid stretch of long afternoons, and because Breanna had said, casually, that it would look good to have something current on the form if a scholarship opened up in the fall.

"Aprons are in the bin," the man said. "Mr. Gupta handles intake at that end. You're on sorting with me and Londyn." Londyn turned out to be the girl from her economics class who never spoke unless called on, already stationed at the far table, tipping a crate of dented cans onto the cloth. Annabelle took the apron and went to stand beside her, feeling the strangeness of being useful at an hour when she was usually still asleep.

The problem revealed itself within ten minutes. A restaurant owner had dropped off four garbage bags of leftover bread, rolls, and half loaves from the night before, but the intake sheet required each donation to be logged with a signature, and the owner had left before anyone could catch her. The distribution opened at nine-thirty. If the bread was not logged, the man in the polo, whose name tag said Daniel, would not put it on the tables, and forty loaves of perfectly good bread would ride back out in a van to somewhere less hungry. "Rules are rules," he said, not unkindly. "No signature, no record, no distribution. That's how it's always been done."

Breanna, who had arrived late and was stacking juice boxes, rolled her eyes. "It's bread, Daniel. It's going to desiccate into bricks by Monday and then it's garbage either way. Just put it out." Annabelle found herself caught between the two positions, or rather holding both at once, because she understood Daniel's caution and also the stupidity of letting good food spoil for the sake of a line on a form. She had spent a semester in economics learning that incentives mattered more than intentions, and here was a case where the rules seemed to punish exactly the behavior the food bank wanted more of.

Mr. Gupta was at the intake desk with the clipboard, so she went to ask him whether there was any middle path. "Call her," he suggested. "The number's on the bakery invoice rubber-banded to one of the bags." He said it the way he said most things, mildly, as though the answer had been sitting on the table the whole time. Annabelle dug through the bags until she found the invoice, and dialed on her own phone with nine-oh-five showing on the wall clock.

The owner answered on the second ring, sounding half awake. When Annabelle explained the missing signature, the woman laughed. "Oh, honey, I should have stayed. I was in a hurry. I'll come sign, I'm ten minutes out." While they waited, Annabelle asked her why she had started donating at all, since she must have worried about someone getting sick off day-old bread and suing the restaurant. "Not really," the owner said. "The Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act, from 1996. It gives food donors limited protection from liability. That's why stores and restaurants like me donate our surplus instead of tossing it. Before I knew that, everything went in the dumpster, I can tell you."

Annabelle stood holding the phone, rearranging something in her head. The law, she thought, was not a set of commands but a nudge, the same way the signature rule was a nudge, and both could be clumsy about it. She still did not know whether Daniel's caution protected people or merely performed protection, and she suspected the honest answer was that it did both, depending on the day. When the owner arrived at nine-twenty and signed the sheet in blue pen, apologizing twice, Annabelle carried the bags to the sorting table herself.

At nine-thirty the doors opened and the line came through, an older woman with a wheeled cart, a father with two kids orbiting him, a teenage boy who took only the bread and nothing else. Londyn worked steadily beside her, and somewhere in the third hour Annabelle noticed her own ennui had lifted entirely, replaced by the simple arithmetic of full boxes and empty tables. Breanna snapped a photo of the bread table for the scholarship form, and Annabelle found she did not care whether it went in.

Around noon a woman took the last loaf, a sourdough with a crack down its crust, and pressed it to her chest like something rescued. "They didn't have this kind last month," she said to Annabelle, already walking toward the exit. "Tell the bread lady I said thank you."

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A straw man is the fallacy of attacking a weaker, distorted version of someone's argument instead of the argument they actually made, while acting as if the two are the same.
story:
The debate unit had been Gibson's territory all semester. Teachers lionized him for it, and even the principal had once stopped him in the corridor to praise his performance at the regional finals, so nobody was surprised when Ms. Hughes asked him to open the discussion on school start times. Nicholas sat two rows back with his notebook open and nothing written in it. He had come to class with a question he had not been able to shake since breakfast: whether changing the schedule would help students who already arrived late, or only the ones who arrived on time and wanted to arrive later. He had not found an answer. He had found instead a set of smaller questions, branching like the streets behind the school, each one depending on the one before it.

"If we push start times back an hour," Gibson said, standing without being asked, "my opponents claim students will just stay up later and gain nothing. But that assumes teenagers have no discipline at all. It assumes we're basically recalcitrant animals who can't manage our own sleep." He paused for the laugh, and got most of one. "So the real question is whether we respect students enough to give them the responsibility."

Nicholas looked down at his notebook. Somebody in the third row, maybe Maely, had raised the staying-up-later point on Tuesday, but she had not said students had no discipline. She had said her brother's school in Calgary had pushed its start time back and his bedtime had drifted to match it. It was a small, careful claim, backed by one household. Gibson had torn into something larger and much weaker, and he was acting as if the two were the same thing. Nicholas felt the unfairness of it in his jaw before he could name it, which bothered him, because feeling something was not the same as being right.

Maely's hand went up. "That's not what I said," she began, but Ms. Hughes was writing something on the board and only nodded, the way adults nod when they have already decided where a class is going. Maely lowered her hand halfway, then all the way. Nicholas watched her thumb the corner of her binder. He thought about the message she had sent him last night, after he had asked her, half joking, whether she thought Gibson could be beaten:

"not on stage. he's too fast. but he's not careful, and careful is the only thing i'm good at. if you ever notice him winning an argument nobody actually started, tell me. that's the door."

He had read it twice and not understood it. He understood it now.

He raised his hand. "Gibson, who said students have no discipline?"

"Plenty of people say it," Gibson said. "There's a whole genre of op-ed."

"Is there anyone in this room who said it?"

Ms. Hughes turned from the board. The class had gone quiet in the particular way it does when someone has stepped off the prepared path. Gibson smiled, the smile of a person who has never needed a second strategy. "You're splitting hairs," he said. "The argument is the same."

"It isn't, though." Nicholas heard his own voice steadier than he felt. "A straw man is the fallacy of attacking a weaker, distorted version of someone's argument instead of the argument they actually made, while acting as if the two are the same." He had not planned to say it as a definition; it came out that way because it was the shape the thing had in his head, and because Maely had once told him that if you can say what a thing is in one breath, you understand it. "Maely said her brother's bedtime moved. You answered as if she'd called us all animals. You won an argument nobody started."

Nobody spoke for a moment. Then Maely said, quietly, "That's the door," and a few people laughed, and even Gibson laughed, though his ears had gone red.

What Nicholas had not expected was that winning the point would feel so unfinished. Ms. Hughes asked him to take the next rebuttal, and he stood and found that he agreed with about half of what Gibson wanted, which made attacking the other half feel like dismantling a house he partly lived in. He said so. He said that if the start time moved, the Calgary evidence was still real, still one household, still worth checking against ours before we spent a year's political capital on it; and that if the start time did not move, respect for students was a poor substitute for sleep. It was not oratory. It was closer to bookkeeping, and he could see Gibson growing bored, and he could see Maely writing something down with the small, contained smile of a person whose door had finally been opened by somebody else.

After class she caught him at the water fountain. "You realize you didn't win," she said.

"I know. I got the fallacy right and the policy wrong, probably."

"Probably," she agreed. "There isn't a right one yet. There's just the honest one."

He thought about that on the bus, turning his pen over in his fingers. He had wanted, for one moment in that classroom, the clean pleasure of watching a strong argument fall, and he had gotten it, and it had lasted about four seconds before the messier question came back: whether the change would help, whether his own mornings would improve, whether a person could hold a position and a doubt about it in the same hand without dropping one. He took out his phone and typed a reply to her old message, then deleted it, then typed it again. "door's open," he wrote. "i'll bring the evidence if you bring the argument." He pressed send before he could make it cleverer, and watched the screen until the word "delivered" appeared beneath it.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine; in RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine and pairs with adenine.
story:
The paper badge read STUDENT DOCENT, CANDIDATE, and Audrey had been staring at it since the bus, as if the laminate might presage how the afternoon would go. Mr. Ramos had said the museum wanted one student from each school to explain the genetics floor to visitors on Saturdays, and that the tryout was simple: at three o'clock, she would be assigned a family, and she would walk them through the double helix. No notes. He would be somewhere on the floor, listening, though he wouldn't say where.

Joe had come along because he claimed he needed to study for the same bio test she did, but within ten minutes of arriving he'd turned pugnacious about it, flicking the edge of her badge and firing questions like a lawyer who already distrusted the witness. "Okay, hotshot. The DNA says G-C-C-A-T. What does the RNA say?"

"Joe, I haven't even found the exhibit yet."

"So find it and then answer."

The genetics floor was cooler than the rest of the building, dim in a way that felt deliberate, the walls printed floor to ceiling with enormous letters. She found the transcription station near the window: a bench, a bowl of paper tiles, and a plastic strip of DNA bolted to the counter like a rail. The strip read, in fat colored letters, A T G C A T G. Beside it, a sign invited her to BUILD THE MESSAGE.

She started laying tiles down the rail, matching each letter with its partner the way the diagram on the wall showed, adenine to thymine, guanine to cytosine. That part had taken her a week to absorb back in September, the idea that the letters weren't arbitrary, that A refused to sit beside anything but T, that G was faithful to C and nothing else. But the sign said the message she was building was RNA, and the tiles in the bowl were a different alphabet. Joe leaned over her shoulder and read it aloud, sounding out the letters like he was deciphering a language he half remembered.

"Wait." He tapped the fourth tile she'd placed, next to the A in the rail. "You put a T there. That's a T. Why is there a T in your RNA?"

She looked at it. She had put a T there. Down the whole line she had written T's, paired neatly against the A's, because that was the rule she knew, and her hand had followed it without consulting the rest of her brain.

"The rule's for DNA," she said slowly. The bowl was still open in front of her. She dug through it, and near the bottom she found tiles she hadn't used at all, cream colored, each stamped with a single letter U. She turned one over in her fingers. "In RNA it's not thymine. It's uracil. So U pairs with adenine, not T." She pulled her T tiles off one at a time and replaced them, and the line read U instead, A U G C A U G, and something in her chest loosened. Joe was quiet for once, watching her fix it, and she thought of her mother reading scripture, the way she insisted the words had to be handled in their own language, that translation was a kind of hermeneutics, an interpretation and not a copy. Audrey had always thought that was a dodge, an excuse for arguing about meaning. Now she wasn't sure. The message had to change to travel.

"Okay," Joe said, checking his phone, "it's three."

The family was already waiting at the helix sculpture: a man, a woman, and a girl about nine who was chewing her sleeve. Audrey started with the ladder of the model, the letters, the pairings, and when she got to the RNA part she slowed down, because the girl had stopped chewing and was looking at her.

"So the DNA stays here," Audrey said, "safe, like the original of something. The RNA is the copy that goes out to do the work. And when the copy gets made, thymine gets swapped out. Every place you'd expect a T, there's a U instead. Uracil. It still pairs with adenine. It still carries the same information. It's just wearing a different letter."

"Like a disguise," the girl said.

"Kind of," Audrey said. "Like a disguise that still tells the truth."

The man asked about the machine that reads the message afterward, the part that turned it into protein, and Audrey started in on codons, three letters at a time, and she was halfway through an example when she noticed the woman's face and stopped. The woman wasn't confused. She was nodding slightly, the way Mr. Ramos nodded when a class discussion was going somewhere he'd planned, and then Audrey saw, over the woman's shoulder, near the archery of the physics floor, the sleeve of a familiar gray jacket retreating behind the pendulum exhibit.

"Anyway," Audrey said, and her voice came out steadier than she felt. "The copy gets read, three letters at a time, and each three letters tells the cell which building block to grab next."

The girl pulled her sleeve out of her mouth. "What happens if the copy gets a letter wrong?"

Audrey looked at the cream colored U tiles still scattered on the bench behind her, at Joe, who shrugged with both eyebrows, and back at the girl's face.

"That," she said, "is a really good question."

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: A binary search of one million sorted items needs at most 20 comparisons, because halving one million twenty times leaves a single item.
story:
Ashton had promised himself he would learn one real thing over the summer before college, and by the third week of July he had narrowed it down to something his older cousin had said at dinner: that you could find any word in a sorted list of a million entries without checking more than twenty of them. He did not believe it. He believed it the way he believed that some people could do long division in their heads, which was to say he believed it happened, somewhere, to other people.

He brought the problem to the public library because his house was loud and because the library had a dictionary so enormous it needed its own stand, a thing the size of a tombstone. He had acclimated to the place over the years, to the smell of warm carpet and the particular silence that was not really silence but a mutual agreement not to be the first one to break it. Mr. Kobayashi, at the front desk, watched him wheel the dictionary over to a table near the window and said nothing, which was his version of approval.

Giuliano arrived first, carrying two sheets of paper Ashton had printed at home, each an identical list of a million fake dictionary words in alphabetical order, generated the night before. Then Libby, who had agreed to referee, though she had made it clear she considered the entire enterprise a scheme. "This is chicanery," she said, settling into a chair with her back very straight. "You made up the words, you made up the rules, and you made up the prize."

"The prize is the last slice of pizza at Nonna's," Ashton said. "It's a real prize."

The race was simple, or it was supposed to be. Giuliano would use what the computer science booklet in his bag called a linear search: start at the top of the list and check each word, one after another, until he found the target. Ashton would use what the same booklet called a binary search, which he had read about twice and half understood. Libby would pick the target word from a hat, literally, a hat, and count each comparison out loud.

The target was "flarnsbury," which sat somewhere in the middle of the first sheet, position 501,204. Giuliano started at the top with visible confidence, dragging his finger down the lines the way he looked for his name on a posted roster. Libby counted. By comparison forty, Ashton still had not touched his sheet, because he was staring at it, trying to remember which half mattered and what to do with the middle. By comparison two hundred, Giuliano was humming.

Ashton opened the dictionary instead, the giant one, because looking at the real thing helped him think. Words in order. He put his hand on the right edge of the page block and imagined letting go of everything before the word he wanted, then everything after, and then doing it again. He went back to his sheet, found the word at the halfway mark, saw his target came after it, and folded the paper in half with a crease so loud that Mr. Kobayashi looked up from the desk. Then he folded it again. Then again. Libby, catching on, began counting for him too, in a different tone, the tone she used for surprising things.

At twenty folds the strip of paper in Ashton's hand was a single line thick, and flarnsbury was on it, and he read it aloud while Giuliano was somewhere around comparison nine thousand, still humming, still confident in the way of a person who had not looked up. Libby declared Ashton the winner. Giuliano demanded to see the folds, unfolded them one by one across the table like a man checking a card trick for wires, and sat back. "That can't be real," he said. "A million words and twenty looks?"

"That's what the booklet says," Ashton said. "Halving a million twenty times leaves you one item." He did not add the part he had not worked out yet, which was how you would ever keep a list that neatly sorted in the first place, or what happened when the data was dirty, or whether the trick survived being translated from paper to code. He had opened his laptop now, a blank file on the screen, and the putative program, which existed so far only as a title and his cousin's dinner-table claim, would have to prove itself the hard way before he trusted it.

Libby ordered the pizza to be delivered to the library steps, out of a kind of ceremonial obligation to the prize, and the three of them sat there in the late light while Ashton typed the first lines and deleted them and typed different ones. Mr. Kobayashi locked the doors behind them and paused on the step, holding his keys. "Twenty, you said," he offered, to no one in particular.

"Nineteen of mine were guesses," Ashton said, still typing. "The twentieth one stuck."

"Then tomorrow you try for nineteen."

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The derivative of a constant is zero, so adding 7 to a function shifts its graph up but leaves its derivative unchanged.
story:
The community centre smelled of chlorine and floor wax, and Autumn would later claim she had chosen the back table by the window for the light, though really she had chosen it because it was farthest from the door and she was planning to leave before anyone noticed she had come. She had told her mother the tutoring session cost nothing, which was true, and that she would definitely go back next week, which was less true. Her mother was at the counter paying the pool fee, counting out a remittance she owed the centre for the swim club fundraiser, coins sliding across the laminate one at a time.

Autumn spread her worksheet on the table. Find the derivative, then use it to locate the maximum. The function was something squared, plus a number, and she had copied it from the board so fast that afternoon that she had no idea whether the number at the end was right. She was certain of very little these days, and she had decided, privately, that this was a kind of wisdom. Her marks had been sliding since winter. Everyone kept saying junior year mattered, and everyone kept saying it in the same jaundiced tone, as though the whole enterprise of her future had already gone wrong somewhere and they were too polite to say where.

"Is this seat taken?" It was Melia from her math class, holding a worksheet of her own, and behind her Elia, who never spoke unless spoken to and sometimes not then. Autumn said no, which was true, though she had been hoping to say yes.

They worked. The room hummed with the pool filter. After ten minutes Elia leaned over Melia's page and frowned, and then leaned over Autumn's page, and said, "That's not what I got."

"Got what?"

"Yours has a plus seven at the end."

Autumn looked. Hers did have a plus seven at the end. Elia's function had no plus seven, nothing at the end at all, and yet when they compared their derivative work, line by line, the derivatives were identical. Every term. Every sign.

"So one of us copied it wrong," Melia said, and Autumn felt the familiar heat rise in her face, because in her experience, historically, statistically, it was her. She was already composing the confession. She had copied it from the board while Ms. Francis was erasing it, half the digits gone before her pencil arrived, and she had invented the seven out of panic, the way she invented most of her certainty.

"You can both be right," Ms. Francis said, passing with a stack of printed schedules. She set them down at the next table and did not stay. She was like that; she offered a sentence the way you'd toss someone a rope, and you either caught it or you didn't.

Melia said, "What's that supposed to mean," but Autumn was already writing. If her function was Elia's function plus seven, then somewhere in the differentiation the seven had to go, and she worked it and reworked it, and the seven went. It just went. There was nothing in the derivative that knew the seven existed. She tried another number, a four, in the margin, and it went too. She wrote a zero next to it and underlined the zero twice, which was more emphasis than she had given anything on a page in months.

"Okay," Elia said slowly, reading upside down. "So we both did it right."

"Both," Autumn said. "Different functions, same derivative." She was careful even as she said it, because she distrusted her own moments of understanding; they had betrayed her before, on exams, at the worst possible times. But the two pages sat side by side on the table, the same derivative written twice in two different hands, and that was not a feeling. That was evidence.

"And the maximum," Melia said, tapping the question. "Where's the maximum?"

Autumn set the derivative equal to zero and solved, and got an x-value, and it was the same x-value Elia got, and Elia's function and hers gave the same height there, except hers was seven higher on the page, and she drew the graph quickly, rough axes, one curve lifted above the other like a card slid up a sleeve. The peak of hers sat directly above the peak of Elia's. Same place. Different height. She sat back and looked at it while the swim class came clattering through in their flip-flops.

Later she would tell her mother that she had understood the whole thing immediately, and that Melia was hopeless, and that she had basically taught Elia. None of that was accurate, and on the walk to the bus stop, holding the worksheet flat against the wind, she amended it in her own head, which was a start: she had understood some of it, after arguing, after being wrong about being wrong. Melia had caught the arithmetic slip first. Elia had laughed once, an actual laugh.

At the bus stop she took out her phone and texted Melia: same time next week? She stood with her thumb over the screen while the bus turned the corner, headlights sweeping the wet road.

"Same time next week," Melia texted back, before the doors even opened.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In The Two Fridas, one Frida wears a white European-style Victorian dress and the other wears a traditional Tehuana dress, a contrast often read as her mixed European and Mexican heritage.
story:
Robert had the printout taped to the wall above his desk, and by eleven on Saturday morning he had read the same paragraph about composition four times without absorbing a word of it. Ms. Clarke-Williams had assigned each student a painting and a single page of formal analysis: colour, composition, symbolism, no biography, no feelings, just what the eye could verify. He had been given The Two Fridas, which meant he was now stuck with two of everything.

Kohen arrived first, dropping his backpack on the bed and standing in front of the printout with his hands in his pockets. "So which one's her?"

"Which one's who?"

"Her. The real one." Kohen tapped the left figure, the one in the white dress with the wide lace skirt. "It's got to be this one. That's how she's looking at you, that's the self-portrait part. The other one's a costume."

Noa came in with two energy drinks and heard the last exchange from the doorway. "Costume," she said, and set the cans down on the desk with a click that Robert felt in his teeth. "The European dress is the costume. She's Mexican."

Kohen turned around fully. "Then why is the Mexican one on the side? Why is she holding the little picture of the guy in her hand?"

"The picture's of Diego, that's the locket she's holding, the vein runs from it. That one's alive. Look at the other one, she's holding the scissors, she cut herself open, the heart's torn."

Robert sat on the edge of the bed and listened while they worked through it, neither giving ground. The morning light came through the blinds in bars across the printout, cutting both women into stripes.

He had seen the painting before, in a textbook two years ago, and he remembered now that in seventh grade he had copied it badly in art class, half an hour before the period ended, and the teacher had told him the two figures were probably just a mirror trick, like a reflection that didn't match. He had believed that for a long time because it was easier than looking. He had drawn both figures in the same blue skirt because he hadn't noticed they were different at all. He had not seen what was on the wall in front of him, which was that the painting was an argument, and that the argument had sides.

"That's not a mirror," he said now. Both of them looked at him. He stood up and went to the printout. "Look, they're holding hands. A reflection doesn't hold your hand."

"So?" Kohen said.

"So it's not one real and one fake." He pointed at the left figure. "This one's in the white European Victorian dress, the whole thing, the lace, the buttons, all of it. And this one's in the Tehuana dress, the traditional Mexican one, the embroidery, the ribbon in the hair." He said the words carefully because he had written them on a notecard the night before and the notecard was still in his pocket. "They're not opposites like real versus fake. They're opposites like two halves of something she actually was."

Noa frowned at the printout. "Mixed heritage," she said slowly.

"European and Mexican, both. That's the reading."

Kohen sat down on the bed and rubbed the back of his neck. "Fine. But the scissors are still on the European side. She's bleeding on that side."

"That part I don't know," Robert said. "That's not in my notes."

For a while none of them said anything. The refrigerator hummed in the kitchen down the hall. Noa opened her can and the hiss filled the room, and Robert went to the desk and pulled his notecards toward him, sorting them into three piles, colour, composition, symbolism, the way Ms. Clarke-Williams had diagrammed on the board. The red of the two hearts went under colour and also under symbolism. The exposed vein went under composition. The sky went under colour, though he hesitated before writing it, because the sky was doing something and he didn't have a pile for that yet.

"It's axiomatic that the blood means pain," Kohen said, reading over his shoulder. "Everybody says blood, pain, done."

"Then everybody's skipping the part where it's connected." Robert drew a line across the notecard from one heart to the other. "One's cut, one's whole, and the vein runs between them. You can't do formal analysis on half a painting."

Noa had gone quiet, and when Robert looked up she was standing close to the printout with her drink forgotten in her hand. "I changed my mind," she said. "Not about the heritage part. About which one's real. I said the Mexican one was real and the dress on the left was a costume, but that's wrong, because if one of them was fake she wouldn't have painted the vein. You don't need to give a costume a working artery."

Kohen exhaled through his nose, which was as close as he came to conceding anything. "So she's both of them and she's not happy about it."

"That's the part I can't prove," Robert said. "I can prove the dresses, I can prove the hands, I can prove the colour temperature shifts from left to right, cold to warm. Whether she liked it is biography and we're not allowed biography." He heard how much the assignment's rule had become his own, and he tested it against what he actually saw, the bare ground behind them, the flat clouds, the two hearts exposed to weather. Some malaise came off the canvas that the word malaise barely covered, but he had no way to put that on paper under formal analysis, so he wrote instead: the horizon line is empty of objects, which is verifiable, and which might do the same work.

He worked until noon while Kohen read a comic on the bed and Noa left, saying something about a shift at the grocery store. At one point Robert looked at what he had written and found a sentence that tried to resuscitate the mirror idea from seventh grade, something about doubling, and he crossed it out with two strokes, because it wasn't his idea, it was a borrowed one, and it didn't fit the evidence of the hands.

When Kohen left, he stood in the doorway with his backpack over one shoulder. "So what do you turn in? Both real?"

"I turn in what I can see," Robert said. "Dresses, hands, vein, sky. The part I'm not sure about goes in the last paragraph, flagged as uncertain."

"Clarke-Williams will love that."

"She asked for analysis, not a verdict."

After the door closed, Robert read the page once more, then took the printout down off the wall and laid it flat on the desk under the lamp so the light fell evenly, no bars from the blinds, both faces lit the same. He got a fresh notecard and wrote the vein question at the top, and under it he wrote the sky.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Ontario high school students must complete 40 hours of community involvement to earn the Ontario Secondary School Diploma.
story:
The cleanup began at nine in the food bank's gravel lot, where someone had abandoned a shopping cart so long ago that moss had claimed its wheels. Victoria arrived with a water bottle, work gloves, and a form folded into quarters in her back pocket. The form mattered more than the gloves. Forty hours of community involvement, or the Ontario Secondary School Diploma stayed out of reach, and Victoria was thirty-one hours short with June arriving like a train she could hear but not see.

"Forty hours," Kadence said, dropping her own form on the folding table with the flourish of someone submitting a winning lottery ticket. "No hours, no OSSD. They really know how to make you love your neighbour." Kadence had, in Victoria's experience, a genius for converting obligations into grievances, and she had already commandeered the last pair of good rakes before anyone else thought to claim them.

Hunter showed up in his father's old gardening boots, laced wrong, and started pulling trash from the fence line without announcing himself. Victoria had known him since grade nine and had never once heard him mention hours. This irritated her in a way she preferred not to examine. On the radio someone had propped on a milk crate, a morning pundit was going on about how young people no longer volunteered, how the requirement had ruined service by making it transactional, and Victoria pulled weeds with slightly more force than the weeds required.

Ms. Chan, who ran the food bank out of what had been a corner store, came out at ten with a tray of lemonade and a look of practiced patience. The building behind her had a penurious kind of dignity: repainted shelves, a hand-lettered sign, a freezer that rattled like it was arguing with itself. "There's more behind the dumpster," she said. "If anyone's ambitious." Victoria, who was not ambitious but was twenty-nine hours short after a Saturday she'd spent at her aunt's instead of the animal shelter, went behind the dumpster.

She found a nest of frozen grocery bags, a bicycle wheel, and a lawn chair missing one leg. She also found a clipboard someone had left on the milk crate, and on it a sheet with Kadence's name at the top and a column of dates stretching back through the winter. Twelve hours in February. Nine in March. Kadence had been in Florida in March; Victoria had seen the photographs, had liked three of them.

She carried the lawn chair to the heap and stood there with it while the radio pundit moved on to property taxes. The honest position, she decided, was not the one she'd arrived with. She had come for the diploma, which was real, and the work was also real, the cold gravel through her knees and the smell of thawed garbage and the fact that people ate because this building existed. Both things could be true at once. What she couldn't decide was whether the second thing excused the first, or whether it mattered, or whether Hunter was simply a better person and the question was her way of avoiding the answer.

She brought the clipboard to Kadence. "You were in Florida in March."

Kadence examined her nails. "My mom signed it."

"That's not what I asked."

"That's what I answered." Kadence took the sheet off the clipboard, folded it once, and put it in her jacket, and that was the end of the conversation, unless it wasn't, unless it was a thing Victoria would be carrying around in her own jacket for the rest of the spring.

At noon, Ms. Chan collected the forms. Victoria's was damp from her pocket and had one honest line on it, four hours, gravel lot, and she watched Ms. Chan initial it without ceremony. Then Ms. Chan looked up. "You're efficient," she said. "Behind the dumpster was on nobody's list for two years." She slid a clipboard across the table, the schedule for the Saturday route, the one that delivered boxes to people who couldn't come in. "I need someone to run it while I do inventory. It's a five-hour shift."

Victoria did the arithmetic before she could stop herself. Thirty-one minus four minus five left twenty-two, and Saturday routes repeated weekly, and she was going to say she'd think about it, she really was.

"We start at nine," Ms. Chan said, already walking away, and Victoria picked up the pen and wrote her name on the line, below two other names, one of which was Hunter's.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: US employers withhold 6.2 percent of an employee's wages for Social Security tax, up to a yearly wage limit.
story:
Jonathan counted the money twice before he said anything, because saying it wrong would have been worse than saying nothing.

He had the receipt spread on the counter of Fontaine's, the little place on Halsted where he'd been bussing tables for three weeks, and the number at the bottom of his paycheck was smaller than the number he'd been carrying around in his head all week. Sixty hours, he was almost sure. Sixty times eight dollars and fifty cents. He'd done that math on the bus, on the walk home, in the shower, the way you do when the money is for something specific. His mother's car needed a new alternator, and she had said, in her careful voice, that she would figure it out, which meant he was supposed to figure it out first.

"Something wrong with it?" Mariane asked. She worked the register on weekday afternoons, and she had a way of asking questions that sounded like she already knew half the answer.

"I don't know yet," Jonathan said. "That's the problem. If something's wrong, I want to know which thing."

He lined up his pay stub next to the check. Federal income tax, he understood; his uncle had warned him about that all through dinner last month, leaning across the mashed potatoes like a man delivering bad news about a distant relative. State tax, fine. But there was a third line, FICA, and it had taken a bite that matched neither of the others, and nobody had ever mentioned it to him at any dinner anywhere.

"It's Social Security," Mariane said, looking over his shoulder. "Everybody pays it."

"Everybody pays what?"

"Six point two percent," she said. "Of your wages. Up to a yearly wage limit, but believe me, you're not near it." She tapped the line with one finger. "It's not a secret. It's just not anything anyone tells you until it happens to them."

Nick came out of the kitchen with a tub of glasses and set it down hard enough to rattle. "You doing taxes at my station?"

"He's discovering America," Mariane said. "Jonathan, some of us have customers."

He folded the stub and put it in his back pocket, but the number came with him through the rest of his shift, through the sweep and the wiping down and the stacking of chairs, because it wasn't the amount that bothered him. It was that the whole system had been running this whole time, taking its six point two percent from every paycheck in the building, up to a yearly wage limit, and he had walked through his entire seventeenth year without once noticing the machinery. That was the part that kept snagging. What else was running quietly in the background of things he thought he understood?

Months earlier, before any of this, he had sat in Ms. Grant's classroom while she tried to get them to care about the difference between a fact and an opinion, and one boy in the back had tried to argue that taxes were theft, and Ms. Grant had refused to vilify him for it, had only asked him to define theft and then define tax and see if the definitions overlapped. Jonathan remembered being annoyed at the time. He'd wanted her to just say who was right. Now he stood at the dish window of a restaurant holding a paycheck that had been trimmed by a percentage he hadn't known existed, and he found he still didn't know who was right, only that the question had a different weight when it was subtracting from something you'd counted on.

What he noticed, closing out his register at the end of the night, was that the arithmetic didn't insult him once he understood it. Six point two percent, of wages, up to a yearly limit. It was clean, even. He could respect a clean number. What he couldn't respect was the silence around it, the way everyone acted like this was a thing you absorbed through the air, part of the vernacular of being grown, like knowing which lane to get in before the exit or how to address a letter to a company. Nobody taught it. You just got shorted and either asked or didn't.

The manager, a heavy man with a red pen he clicked like a metronome, came by while Jonathan was restocking napkins. "How's it going, kid?"

"Fine," Jonathan said. Then, because the word felt like a lie the second it left him: "Actually, can I ask you something? If I work more hours, does that percentage stay the same?"

"Until you hit the yearly wage limit," the manager said. "Which, no offense, at eight fifty an hour, you will not."

The manager laughed and moved on, and Jonathan laughed too, a little, and then stopped, because something had settled in him that hadn't been there at the start of the shift. He didn't love the deduction. He wasn't grateful for it, exactly. But he understood it now, understood its shape and its ceiling and its arithmetic, and that understanding felt like something he owned in a way the money, apparently, did not. Whether it was fair was a separate question, and he was beginning to suspect it was the kind you had to keep answering your whole life instead of answering once.

Mariane clocked out beside him at ten. Outside, under the green awning, she counted her tips with the unembarrassed efficiency of someone who'd been doing it since she was fifteen.

"You know what's funny," she said, folding the bills into her pocket. "The first time I got a check I cried. I thought they'd stolen from me."

"What did you do?"

"Nothing. My mom explained it over dinner and I got over it." She shrugged into her jacket. "You're taking it better than I did."

Jonathan looked back through the glass at the empty tables, the chairs upside down, the lights going off one section at a time. "I'm not taking it better," he said. "I'm just taking it slower."

Mariane smiled at that, or at something past him, and they walked to the bus stop together, her counting coins into the fare box when it came.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A standard piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black.
story:
The garage smelled of motor oil and old cardboard, and in the middle of it stood a piano that had belonged to Lea's grandmother, an upright with a scarf of dust along the lid. Her father had cleared the workbench to make room for it three weeks ago, the day after Ms. Kobayashi announced the spring showcase and said, in that level way of hers, that anyone who wanted a slot needed to pass a placement check by Friday. Lea had said yes before she could think better of it, which was how most of her decisions got made, and now Friday was four days away and her hands still felt like borrowed gloves.

"Play the C scale again," said Kailee, who sat cross-legged on an overturned milk crate with a stopwatch on her phone. "But this time don't stop in the middle like the bench is electric."

"I didn't stop in the middle."

"You stopped at F. Every time. It's like you and F have a subpoena out on each other."

Lea laughed despite herself, which broke her concentration, and she put her hands in her lap. The garage had one window, high and grimy, and the afternoon light came through it in a flat gray sheet that made everything look like a photograph taken just before something happened. She had learned that from Carlos, who wanted to be a filmmaker and described the world in camera angles. He had claimed the folding chair behind her and kept saying noncommittal things like "interesting choice" whenever she hit a wrong note, which was less helpful than he seemed to think it was.

The problem, as far as Lea could name it, was that she had two teachers in her head and they disagreed. Ms. Kobayashi wanted precision, fingers curved, wrists level, every note placed like evidence at a trial. But Lea's grandmother, in the single summer Lea had watched her play before she died, had seemed to pour herself over the keys, swaying, humming, occasionally hitting wrong notes and smiling at them as if they were guests who'd arrived at the wrong house but were welcome anyway. Lea wanted both. She wanted to be correct and she wanted to be free, and she could not yet verbalize why she believed those were two different things, or whether they had to be.

"Count something for me," she said suddenly, turning on the bench. "The keys. While I play. I keep losing my place when I look down."

"Count the keys," Kailee said. "Sure. Extremely normal request." But she got up and stood at the piano anyway, tapping each one with one finger like a clerk counting money. "Fifty-two white," she reported. "Unless I skipped one, in which case, fifty-one."

"Fifty-two's right," Carlos said from his chair. "It's a standard piano. Fifty-two white and thirty-six black. My cousin has one. I counted it at Christmas because I was bored, and my aunt said it was a standard piano, eighty-eight keys altogether."

Lea did the arithmetic in her head, and it came out even, which pleased her in a way she couldn't quite explain. She looked at the keyboard again and noticed, for the first time really noticed, how the black keys clustered in twos and threes, and how the same pattern repeated up and down like a fence with alternating posts. She had been playing for three weeks and had never once looked at the whole landscape, only at the particular key her finger was supposed to find next. "Say that again," she said. "Fifty-two and thirty-six."

"Fifty-two and thirty-six," Carlos said. "Eighty-eight total. Why, does it matter?"

She didn't answer, because she wasn't sure yet whether it mattered or how. But she put her hands back on the keys and played the scale, and this time when she reached F she didn't stop, because F was just the fourth white key after the twos-and-threes pattern started over, and knowing where she was in the whole made her less afraid of the part. Was that what Ms. Kobayashi meant by precision, she wondered, not stiffness but simply knowing the map? And was that what her grandmother had, all along, a map so well learned she could wander on it?

The stopwatch on Kailee's phone buzzed. "Two minutes," Kailee said. "You went all the way up and back without stopping. That's the first time."

"Play it like you played it just now," Carlos said, "but on Friday, in front of her."

Lea looked at the eighty-eight keys, all of them, white and black, and at her own small hands resting on eight of them. Four days. She lifted her wrists, set them down, and began again from the beginning.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: In gleaning programs, food bank volunteers harvest crops that remain in farm fields after the main harvest, food that would otherwise go to waste.
story:
The soup kitchen smelled of onions and dish steam, and Julia stood at the counter cutting bread until her thumb ached from pressing the knife. She had signed up because her mother had found the form and left it on her desk without a word, which was its own kind of sentence. Two Saturdays of community service, the school required, and she had waited until the last possible weekend, so here she was, halving rolls while a man with burn-scarred hands carried trays past her to the tables.

"First time?" the man asked. When she nodded, he pointed a spatula at the notice pinned above the sink, a handwritten sheet about Saturday's farm run. "You should come to that instead. It's better work. You'll see where the food comes from."

The notice said the volunteers would go out to the fields after the main harvest had already finished. Julia read it twice. She had assumed, without ever examining the assumption, that a food bank was a place where food arrived in boxes and left in bags, a building with a door on each side. That the food might still be standing in the ground a day earlier was a thought she had never had, and it unsettled her the way true things sometimes did, arriving with no ceremony and rearranging everything behind them.

She texted Anton that night. His reply came while she was brushing her teeth: "my grandma used to do that, going behind the combines. she called it gleaning. old word." Julia sat on the edge of the tub with her phone, holding the word. Gleaning. It sounded biblical, or at least rural in a way her suburb was not, a word that had survived because the thing it named kept happening, harvest after harvest, field after field.

On Saturday, Mr. Fischer drove the van, and Jayden rode shotgun, narrating everything in a running commentary that Julia suspected was nerves. The farm was forty minutes out, and the farmer met them at the gate with a wave and a shrug that seemed to augur either a good morning or a resigned one; his face gave no verdict. The field behind him had already been harvested, the main crop taken, but the ground was littered with squash, misshapen or undersized or simply missed by the machines, all of it left behind in the rows.

"None of this gets picked up," the farmer said. "What you bag goes to the food bank. What you don't, rots." He said it without drama, the way you'd mention weather. Jayden asked why the machines missed so much, and the farmer said something about size and shape and speed, and then he handed out gloves and the conversation turned practical, which was its own mercy. Julia knelt in the cold dirt and began to gather.

The work was simple and repetitive and, after the first half hour, oddly absorbing. Pick up the squash, wipe the mud off, put it in the crate, move down the row. Mr. Fischer worked two rows over, moving slowly and steadily, and at one point he called across to them, "You know there's a colloquialism about this, something about gleaning the truth?" Nobody knew whether he had it right, and he laughed and went back to picking, unbothered by his own uncertainty. Julia noticed that about him, that he could hold a half-remembered thing loosely instead of clenching it.

Her grandmother, she remembered suddenly, had once spent an afternoon salvaging a dinner from a failed grocery run, and when Julia had asked why she didn't just throw it all out and start over, her grandmother had been obdurate about it, refusing flatly, saying waste was waste no matter whose money bought it. At the time Julia had thought this was a weakness of old people, an inability to let things go. Now, kneeling in a field full of food that would otherwise rot, she wasn't sure it was a weakness at all. She wasn't sure it was entirely a strength, either; there was something exhausting in it, a refusal that could harden into its own kind of blindness. She held both thoughts the way she held the squash, one in each hand, and did not drop either.

At the end of the row she found a squash split open by the harvester, its orange flesh exposed to the cold air, already darkening at the edges. It was still mostly good. She stood there with it, weighing whether a mostly good thing counted as good enough, and heard Anton down the row calling her name, holding up a crate nearly full. "This one's the last of it," he said. "Fischer says we're done when this one's full." Julia looked at the split squash in her hands, then down the row behind her, where she could see at least a dozen more she'd missed, small and pale against the dark soil. She put it in her crate and walked back toward the van, and behind her the row went on.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude, about 95 degrees Celsius at 5,000 feet, so boiled foods take longer to cook.
story:
Morgan had claimed the dinner before anyone could assign it, which surprised her father enough that he handed over the stove without argument. Two nights of sandwiches and burned hot dogs had made the family quietly desperate, and she had watched enough of her mother's cooking to feel, if not ready, then at least stubborn. Pasta with the jar of sauce and the last of the parmesan. Simple. Forgiving. Or so she believed.

The campsite sat high on a shelf of rock above the lake, and while the water came to a boil she stood mesmerized by the way it rolled against the dented pot, the surface breaking and reforming in the low light. Her father had driven them up two days of switchbacks to get here, and the elevation was a fact she carried in her body without naming it, a lightness in her breathing she kept deciding was imagined.

She read the box, as her mother did at home. Eleven minutes. She set the timer on her phone and dropped the noodles in, and Livia texted her a photo from a party she had chosen not to attend, and Morgan typed back a thumbs up and felt the small somatic weight of that choice settle somewhere between her ribs and her stomach. Eleven minutes passed. She pulled a strand out, blew on it, bit it. It cracked between her teeth like a raw bean.

"Give it a few more," her father said, not unkindly, poking at the pot on his way past with firewood. That was the problem with him, she thought. He never said what he meant. A few more meant I told you so, or it meant nothing at all, and she couldn't decide which was worse.

She gave it four more minutes, then six. The strands softened at the edges but stayed rigid at their centers, pale and wrong, and the sauce was already heating in the second pot and her brother had started the low drumming of fingers on the picnic table that meant hunger turning into grievance. She fished out another piece. Still hard. The water had been boiling the entire time, a steady rolling boil, the strongest the little stove could manage, and it had been boiling for twenty minutes now, and the pasta was refusing all of it.

"Kyan," she said into her phone, walking a few steps toward the trees, keeping her voice flat so no one would hear the wobble underneath. "Kyan, you did chemistry. If water's boiling, like fully boiling, and pasta won't soften, what is that."

"Honestly? Probably I'd say you didn't salt it enough," Kyan said, and then, when she said nothing, "Or you're high up. Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude. Like at 5,000 feet, water boils at about 95 degrees Celsius, so boiled foods take longer to cook. Where even are you?"

She looked back at the campsite. Her brother was stacking kindling he'd been told not to touch. Her mother sat with the map across her knees. The stove hissed. She said a quick thanks, hung up, and stood a moment in the cold coming down off the ridge, because something in her wanted to have figured it out herself and now she never would.

At the picnic table she opened the sauce and stirred the noodles and made herself say it out loud. "The water boils cooler up here. We're at altitude, so it boils at about 95 degrees instead of 100, and the pasta needs more time." She kept her eyes on the pot. "Maybe another ten minutes."

Her father stopped with the firewood in his arms. "Where'd you hear that?"

"Kyan." A beat. "And I checked the trailhead sign. We're above 5,000 feet." The second part was true, though she had only read the sign after the call, walking back, doing the arithmetic in reverse so the fact would look discovered rather than given.

Nobody said anything for a second, and then her mother said, "Then we wait," and turned back to the map, and Morgan understood that this was the closest thing to a verdict she would get. She returned to the stove. The wait itself became the dinner, in a way. Her brother gave up drumming and toasted marshmallows over the fire her father built, feeding the flames with the patience of someone with nowhere else to be, and Morgan stood guard over the pot, testing a strand every few minutes, refusing to guess twice.

When it finally gave, it gave all at once, the last hardness dissolving between her teeth, and she drained the noodles and folded in the sauce and carried the pot to the table with both hands, steam rising off it into the dusk. It was not the dinner she had planned, and it was later than she had promised, and she still didn't know whether her father's silence that evening meant approval or the absence of it. But her brother took seconds without being asked, and from the next site over, Ms. Chanthavong, the retired teacher who had lent them the lantern their first night, called across the dark, "Smells better than anything I've managed all week," and Morgan laughed once, surprised by the sound of it.

"Recipe's mostly patience," she called back, and lifted the pot to scrape the last of it onto her brother's plate.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: On the practical driving test in Great Britain, parallel parking at the side of the road is one of the reversing manoeuvres the examiner may ask a candidate to do.
story:
The afternoon light came flat and grey through the windows of the sixth form common room, and Simon sat with the highway code open on his knee, not reading it so much as letting his eyes rest on the page. His test was in eleven days. He had booked it in a rush of confidence back in March, when bay parking had begun to feel almost easy, and now the confidence had thinned into something more careful.

"You're doing the face," Karis said, dropping into the chair opposite him with her coffee. "The worried face."

"I'm fine. I've done the bay park maybe forty times." He turned the booklet towards her, though the page meant nothing to her. "It's the other one."

Harman arrived, late as always, shaking rain off his jacket. "The other one what?"

"Parallel parking. At the side of the road. I never practise it because I thought the bay was the real test, but my instructor said the examiner chooses." He heard his own voice speed up and steadied it. "On the practical test, parallel parking at the side of the road is one of the reversing manoeuvres the examiner may ask a candidate to do. May. That's the word. It's not guaranteed either way."

"So practise it," Harman said, in the tone of someone for whom problems were simply undeclared solutions. "My dad will take you out. He owes me for washing his car anyway."

That evening they drove to the quiet street behind the retail park, where terraced houses sat shoulder to shoulder and nobody parked after six. The rain had stopped and the tarmac shone, and Simon sat in the driver's seat of Harman's dad's car with his hands at ten and two, waiting. The first attempt he overcorrected, riding the kerb with the back wheel, and the second he finished a full metre from the kerb, a gap you could have parked a bicycle in.

"Again," said Harman's dad from the passenger seat, in a voice so calm it was almost torpid, though Simon could see him bracing a hand on the dash at each approach.

On the fifth attempt the car slid into the space with a soft, surprising rightness, close to the kerb, evenly spaced between the two imaginary cars. Simon sat without moving, feeling his pulse slow. It felt less like a triumph than like a reprieve, one granted by luck as much as by skill, and he knew the difference mattered.

They drove out to the ring road while the light lasted, because merging had been his other fear, the one he confessed only to Harman's dad on the slip road. Up the ramp, mirror, signal, glance, and then the moment of decision when the traffic in the near lane was a wall of headlights and he had to find the seam. The first time he slowed too much and Harman's dad said gently, "You can't creep onto a motorway," and the second time Simon pressed the accelerator and the car folded into a gap between a van and a hatchback, and nobody died, and nobody even honked.

Later, in the common room before their free period ended, Ms. Fischer stopped by their table to collect the worksheets nobody had collected and asked, in her offhand way, how the driving was going. Simon found himself explaining both approaches without planning to: the way he used to think, that you drilled one manoeuvre until it was automatic and then you were safe, and the way he thought now, that the examiner might ask for anything, so safety was really the ability to meet whatever showed up. "Both of them are partly true," he said. "The drilling is what made the parallel park possible today. But it wasn't enough on its own."

Karis looked up from her phone. "So which is it, then?"

"Both. You practise the specific thing until it stops being a specific thing, and then you practise being ready for the thing you didn't practise." He laughed at himself a little. "I don't know if that's a real principle or just what I'm telling myself before the test."

"It's a real principle," Ms. Fischer said, gathering the last worksheet, "but don't quote me."

On the day itself, the examiner walked around the car once, clipped the seatbelt, and said, in a voice like a man reading a shopping list, "Pull up on the left here, please, and reverse back two car lengths." Simon signalled, checked, drew in against the kerb, and put his hand on the handbrake. The street ahead was long and quiet, lined with the same shoulder-to-shoulder terraces he had learned on, and he said, "Ready when you are."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: In the UK, a driver who passes the test in an automatic car may drive only automatic cars, and must pass a manual test to drive a manual car.
story:
The instructor's car was silver and small and smelled of air freshener shaped like a pine tree, and Zoey sat in the driver's seat before she had ever turned a key anywhere. Mr. Grant, laconic in the way of men who had said the same things for twenty years, adjusted the mirror on his side and told her to check hers. On the dashboard, between the two seats, the gear lever ended in a flat gate with P and D and R printed in white, and no third pedal at her feet.

She had chosen this car herself, or believed she had. Two weeks ago she had sat at the kitchen table with the driving school's website open, comparing prices, and clicked automatic because the list of things to worry about got shorter. One less pedal, one less system, one less way to stall at a roundabout with a queue building behind her. Her mother had said nothing at the time, which Zoey understood now might have been its own kind of comment, because the car in the driveway, the one with the dented rear wing and the smell of the dog, was manual. Her mother had driven it for fifteen years, heel-and-toe on the pedals, hand falling on the gearstick like it lived there.

"All right," Mr. Grant said. "Seatbelt. Start the engine. Foot on the brake."

She did it. The engine made its quiet electric-sounding hum and the street ahead, a suburban avenue of low hedges and parked vans, waited for her.

"Into D. Handbrake down. Now take your foot off the brake, gently, and let the car creep."

It crept. That was the strange part. Without asking anything of her, the car began to move, and the curb curved away toward the corner in a long line that reminded her of asymptotes in maths, curves approaching a line forever without touching, close and closer and never quite there. She steered toward it anyway and the wheels tracked along the kerb at a polite distance, and Mr. Grant said "good" once, the way a person stamps a form.

Halfway down the street a boy from her year, Bilal, was walking on the pavement with his headphones in, and he raised a hand without breaking stride. She waved back through the windscreen. Bilal had passed his test in the spring, in his uncle's manual Micra, and had been unbearable about it for exactly one week before going quiet. "It's not to aggrandize myself," he had told her once, when Gwen accused him of learning manual just so he could say he had. "It's so I can drive anything. Any car, any time." She had thought that was a distinction without a difference. Now, crawling along at twelve miles an hour, she thought about her mother's dented manual in the driveway, and how she would not be driving it home from this kind of lesson, and she began to turn the thought over.

"When I pass," she said, watching the road, "in this car. Then I can drive any car, right? Both kinds?"

Mr. Grant was quiet for the length of two houses. "In an automatic, no," he said. "Pass your test in an automatic, the licence covers automatics. You'd have to pass another test, a manual test, before you can drive a manual."

The kerb slid past. A sprinkler ticked across someone's lawn and left rainbows in the spray, and Zoey held the wheel steady and did the arithmetic. Not money, exactly, though money was in it. It was that the easy choice now had a shape, a boundary drawn around it, and everything outside that boundary required doing the whole thing twice. She remembered Gwen saying something like this at lunch, weeks ago, a sentence about her cousin's licence that Zoey had filed away as boring paperwork talk. She hadn't connected it to the click of her own mouse at the kitchen table, the one small decision made while her mother washed up in the next room.

"Turn left at the end," Mr. Grant said. "Signal first."

She signaled. She slowed, checked the mirror, turned the wheel, and the car swung around the corner obediently, and it was so easy, that was the thing. The ease was real. No stalling, no rolling back on the hill by the parade of shops, no lurching through the gears while a van driver shook his head at her. Twice the work later for half the trouble now, or half the trouble now and a locked door at home. She could not decide which way round to put it, and the street offered no opinion, just more hedges, more parked cars, a man watering baskets outside the corner house.

"Can I change?" she asked. "For the next lesson. To the manual car."

Mr. Grant looked at her, then out at the road. "We can do that," he said. "Mind the cyclist."

The cyclist passed on her outside, close enough that she felt the small wind of it, and she held the wheel still and let the automatic carry her on down the street, for this one morning, toward the parking bay outside the school.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: Long or repeated exposure to sounds at or above 85 decibels can cause hearing loss, and the damaged hair cells in the human inner ear do not grow back.
story:
The ringing in Vincent's ears had lasted two days after the last show, and he had told himself it was fine, that everyone's ears rang after standing beside the speakers at the Beanfield, that Marc-Olivier's ears were ringing too and Marc-Olivier wasn't worried. That was Monday. By Wednesday, when the ringing had faded to a thin hum he could only hear in the quiet of the library, he was still telling himself it was fine, but he had started to notice that he said it out loud more often than a person who was actually fine would need to.

"You're doing the thing," Monica said, dropping her tray beside his in the cafeteria. "The thing where you repeat something until it becomes true."

"I'm not doing a thing. My ears are fine. Anyway, the second show is Friday, and the tickets are nonrefundable, and Marc-Olivier has been talking about this band since September like it's a religious pilgrimage." The whole school had begun to lionize the group, honestly, kids who'd never heard a single track wearing the tour shirt, and Vincent had let himself get swept along because being swept along was easier than admitting he'd spent his savings.

"Two shows in one week," Monica said. "Standing where, again?"

"Near the front. It's better near the front." He said it with the certainty of someone quoting a law, which was the problem, because the certainty was borrowed and the ears were his own.

After last period he took the long route past the nurse's office, telling himself he was avoiding the crowded stairwell.
