On the wall outside there was a rack of pamphlets nobody ever took, and one had a photo of a boy about his age holding a phone up at a concert. Vincent read it standing up, coat half on. Long or repeated exposure to sounds at or above 85 decibels could cause hearing loss. He looked up 85 decibels on his phone right there in the hallway: it was about the level of heavy traffic, and concerts ran far past it. The last line of the pamphlet was the one he read twice. The damaged hair cells in the human inner ear did not grow back. Not healed slowly, not recovered with rest. Did not grow back, the way other things in the body did.

He showed the pamphlet to Monica at her locker before practice. "It's the hair cells," he said. "In the inner ear. When they're gone, they're gone. Like, permanently."

"So wear earplugs."

"If I wear earplugs Friday, Marc-Olivier's going to say something. He already called my seat cushion 'a phenotype for people who nap in class.' You don't know what he's like about the front row. He called it sacred ground." Vincent knew even as he said it that this was a small objection dressed up as a large one, the way he knew the hum in his ears was still there under the noise of the hallway, patient, waiting for him to be quiet.

Mr. Littlechild, who taught geography and supervised the recycling bins Vincent had volunteered for to pad his college applications, was locking his classroom when Vincent wandered past Thursday after school. Vincent asked, as casually as he could manage, whether Mr. Littlechild still went to shows, because everyone knew he had played bass in some pelagic-themed prog band in the nineties, albums with whales on the cover, a whole era of his life the students would never let him forget.

"Still do," Mr. Littlechild said. "Loud ones." He pulled something small from his jacket pocket and set it in Vincent's palm: a pair of foam plugs, orange, unglamorous. "Lost enough of the high end that I can't hear my own daughter when she talks softly. I'm not telling you what to do with these. I'm just saying they fit in a pocket."

Friday came faster than a decision should, and Vincent still hadn't made one, because making one meant choosing between two versions of himself and admitting the previous one had been wrong. He met Marc-Olivier outside the venue with the plugs buried at the bottom of his bag, under a granola bar, where they could plausibly be forgotten.

They got to the front, against the barrier, and the opener hit the stage like a wall, and Vincent felt the sound in his teeth. Beside him Marc-Olivier was shouting something, grinning, and the speakers were close enough that Vincent could see the cones shaking. His ears were going to ring again. That was simply what was going to happen, unless. He ducked under the crush toward the back of the crowd, found a pocket of relative stillness near the sound desk, and dug the plugs out of his bag with shaking fingers. He rolled them, waited for them to expand, and stood there in the half-dark while the band he'd paid too much to lionize thundered on without him at the barrier.

Marc-Olivier found him during the changeover, sweating, indignant. "You left sacred ground for the nosebleeds?"

"Front row's still there," Vincent said. "It doesn't expire." He pointed at the plugs in his ears, and then, when Marc-Olivier cupped a hand behind his ear and leaned in, he pulled one out and said, louder than he meant to, "The hair cells don't grow back, man. They just don't."

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Supercompensation is the idea that the body gets fitter during recovery after training, when it rebuilds beyond its previous level, not during the workout itself.
story:
The chain-link gate to the diamond still sang in the wind after Morgan latched it, a thin metallic whine that she had never noticed before this summer, when the field had become the place she came to be alone with a stopwatch and her own disappointment. She set her cleats on the bench, pulled a water bottle from her bag, and read the numbers she had written on her wrist in ballpoint: sixty-yard times, one each morning for eleven straight days. The first said 7.41. The last said 7.58. Eleven days of sprinting until her hamstrings shook, and she was getting slower.

Mikayla arrived at noon, glove hanging off two fingers, the way she carried everything, as if permanently on her way to setting it down. "You're here again," she said. "You were here yesterday. And the day before. My mom asked if you'd moved in."

"Coach needs speed by September," Morgan said. "So I'm running speed."

"That's not how speed works, though. My brother swears by his off days. He calls them the whole point."

Morgan had dismissed that kind of talk all summer, the way she dismissed anything that sounded like an excuse dressed up as wisdom. But driving home that afternoon she found herself thinking of her mother's bookshelf, the exercise-physiology textbook from a nursing degree never finished. She had pulled it down once before, in the spring, looking for a diagram of the rotator cuff. This time she sat on the kitchen floor and read until the light went orange across the linoleum.

There was a word in the third chapter, and the word was supercompensation. The body, the book said, gets fitter during recovery after training, when it rebuilds beyond its previous level, not during the workout itself. She read the sentence four times. She thought of the eleven numbers on her wrist and felt something between relief and humiliation, the particular sting of discovering that effort and progress were not the same currency. She had been spending one and billing herself in the other.

She remembered being nine, at this same diamond, when her father would pitch to her until dark. One evening she had swung until her hands blistered, and he had closed the bucket of balls and said, "That's enough for today. The rest is where it sinks in." She had thought he meant the muscle memory, the sleeping brain filing things away. Now she wondered whether he had meant something closer to what the textbook meant, whether he had known all along and never dressed it up as a lesson. It bothered her a little, how much the adults in her life seemed to know and hold back, and it bothered her more that she had never thought to historicize her own routine, to ask where it had come from, whose postulate it was that more was always more. She had simply inherited the assumption that a stopwatch was a moral instrument.

The next morning she did what she had never done on purpose: she drew a grid on a fresh page, seven columns, and wrote easy, hard, rest, hard, easy, rest across the week. She penciled in warm-ups before everything, ten minutes of dynamic work she'd always skipped as a formality. On the rest days she wrote nothing at all, and the blank squares looked, at first, like laziness rendered in graph form. She kept the page anyway.

By Thursday she was restless enough to text Mikayla, who replied with a photo of herself on a porch doing a crossword, captioned "day of gains." Morgan laughed, then felt the strange freedom of a discipline she could actually follow, a plan with empty rooms built into it.

Ten days later she stood at the chain-link gate again, the wind working the same thin note out of the metal. Mikayla held the stopwatch. Morgan had spent the morning's warm-up slowly, deliberately, the way the grid said to, and now she set her feet in the grass beyond first base.

"Supercompensation," Morgan said, crouching into her start. "That's the word. Blame my mom's textbook."

"Whatever it's called," Mikayla said, thumb on the button, "just run."

She ran.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: With typical use, about 13 in 100 people relying only on male condoms for a year have an unintended pregnancy, mostly because condoms are not used correctly every time.
story:
The kitchen smelled of burnt toast and lemon dish soap, and Nicolas had spread the peer-health binder across the table so that it covered the salt shaker, two mugs, and Augustin's phone. He had volunteered for this because Ms. Rowe had asked him quietly after class, in the corridor, away from the boys who snickered, and because he had frozen that day in the gym when a ninth-grader asked him what happens at a clinic and he had said, "Um, they help you," which was the same thing you'd say about a shoe store.

"So you have to actually explain it," Augustin said, peeling an orange in one long spiral, the way his grandmother had taught him. "Not just point at the binder."

"I can explain it. I'm explaining it right now." Nicolas turned the binder around so the page faced them. "Consent. Contraception. Testing. Three stations, three minutes each."

Ernest sat with his arms crossed at the end of the table. He had been dour all afternoon, since the rain had cancelled his track meet, and he had announced that he was only here because his mother had made him come, though he had taken the seat closest to the cocoa Nicolas was heating on the stove.

"Fine," Nicolas said. "Station one. Consent is a yes you can say freely, and you can take it back, and silence isn't it. If someone's been drinking, you wait. If you're not sure they'd say it sober and awake, that's your answer." He said it to the window because it was easier than saying it to their faces, and the window gave him back a blurry version of himself holding a wooden spoon.

"That's decent," Augustin said. "Say the last part again, the drinking part. Slower. The ninth-graders are going to be nervous."

Nicolas said it again, slower, and this time looked at Augustin, who nodded the way people nod when something has actually landed.

"Station two," Ernest said, with the tone of a boy hoping to speed things along. "The condom thing. Just read the box number off and done."

"That's what I thought too." Nicolas tapped the page, where Ms. Rowe had highlighted a row of a handout she'd left in his mailbox with a sticky note reading, Know this one cold. "But listen. With typical use, about thirteen in a hundred people relying only on male condoms for a year have an unintended pregnancy. Mostly because condoms aren't used correctly every time." He had read it four times on the bus, and it had gotten stranger each time, not because it was complicated but because it wasn't what the box implied at all.

"Thirteen," Augustin said, letting a segment of orange fall out of his hand onto the binder. "That's way more than I thought. Way more than anyone thinks."

"Right, so that's the whole job of station two. Nobody's telling them condoms don't work. We're telling them the real-world number so they can decide, and so they know why doing it right every single time matters." Nicolas glanced at Ernest. "You look like you want to argue."

"I don't want to argue." Ernest turned his mug in a slow circle on the table. "Last year somebody gave the ninth-graders a talk like this and it was a joke, is all. Everyone laughed the whole time and nobody learned anything, and then a girl in my brother's class ended up in a situation she didn't want." He looked up. "If you're doing this, do it like it matters."

The cocoa had begun to skin over on top. Nicolas poured three cups without asking, and set Ernest's down first, closest to his hand. "I'm sorry," he said. "For the shoe-store answer, in the gym. I know you were there." Ernest had been there, near the back, and Nicolas had laughed it off afterward in the changing room to cover how stupid he'd felt. He hadn't thought about it as something needing reparation until now, but that was what it was, and the apology sat between them on the table until Ernest picked up his cup.

"Station three," Ernest said, after a while. "Clinics."

"Testing." Nicolas turned the page. "You can walk in or book online. You don't need a parent with you at our age. They ask what you want tested for, they explain first, and you can change your mind at any point, same as anything else. It's confidential unless you're in danger, and if something does come back positive, most of it is treatable and they tell you exactly what happens next." He paused. "That's the part the kid in the gym actually asked me. What happens. And the honest answer is: an appointment, some questions, maybe a swab or a blood draw, and then you know. Knowing is the whole point."

Augustin raised his orange-sticky hand like they were back in Ms. Rowe's classroom. "One thing you haven't figured out. What if somebody asks you something you don't know? Some number, some method, whatever."

"Then I say I don't know and I find out and I tell them after." Nicolas stacked the mugs, wiped the binder clean of orange juice with the dishcloth, and closed it. "Ms. Rowe says that's allowed. She says the only wrong answer is the made-up one."

The rain had started again against the kitchen window, and Ernest pulled his hood up but didn't stand. "Run the consent station on me," he said. "The ninth-graders are going to try to trip you up. Ask you about the stuff that's awkward."

"Like what?"

Ernest put on a flat, bored voice, chin lifted, doing an impression of every fourteen-year-old boy Nicolas had ever met. "So if she doesn't say no, that means yes, right?"

"Silence isn't a yes," Nicolas said, without looking at the binder, and reached over to slide the cocoa closer to Ernest's hand.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During Japan's Buddhist festival of Obon, families light fires to welcome the spirits of ancestors home, and at the end many float lanterns down rivers to guide the spirits back.
story:
The path up to the cemetery was steep, and Hailey's aunt climbed it without waiting, a bucket and a bundle of grass in one hand. At the top, rows of narrow stone markers stood shoulder to shoulder like a crowd waiting for something. Her grandfather had been in the ground here since March, and in all the years before that he had existed for Hailey mostly as postcards, laconic things with weather on them and a single question at the bottom: Still playing violin? She had eleven of them in a shoebox at home, and she had answered perhaps four.

Her aunt knelt at the marker, scrubbed the stone, poured water over it. Then she set a small pile of dried grass and lit it. The flame caught and leaned in the wind. "During Obon," her cousin said in English, for Hailey's benefit, "the fires call the spirits home. His spirit comes back to the house for the festival." Hailey watched the smoke thin out over the stones. It was strange to think of something arriving when the body was right there beneath her shoes, but her aunt spoke about it the way she spoke about trains, as plain schedule.

Hailey had told Lila almost nothing about the trip. That morning, walking behind her relatives, she had taken out her phone. Lila's text said: you said you barely knew him, why are you doing all this funeral stuff for a stranger? Hailey had typed three replies and deleted each one. The veracity of Lila's charge was what stung: he was, in most senses, a stranger. He had come to visit twice, once when she was six. She had a memory of him holding a firefly in his cupped hands, telling her to look, and she had refused, sulking about something, and had never thought about it again until the postcards started.

That night at the house there were paper lanterns folded flat on the tatami, and her aunt wrote a name on one in ink. Her cousin explained that the festival ended tomorrow, and at the end families floated lanterns down the river to guide the spirits back. "Back where?" Hailey asked. Her cousin only tapped the paper. Tomorrow at dusk, she said; the last night; after that, nothing until next year.

Hailey had decided she would not go. It seemed like a performance of grief she had no right to give, a costume borrowed from people whose loss was real. She told her aunt this at breakfast, in her careful, slow Japanese, and her aunt did not argue, only said, "Then help me clean the altar," and Hailey spent the morning washing small cups and resetting the fruit, and somewhere in the middle of arranging persimmons she understood that she had been trying to exonerate herself, that skipping the river was a way of saying she had nothing to answer for, when in fact the shoebox of unanswered postcards said otherwise.

She changed her mind while drying a cup. It was not that she believed her grandfather would ride a paper boat down a river. It was that the fire her aunt had lit at the grave and the lanterns on the water were a single sentence spoken across a week, and if she stayed home she would never know the end of it, and neither would he, in whatever way mattered. She asked her cousin, "What time do we leave?" and her cousin, who had been laconic all summer in a way that suddenly looked like patience, said, "Five."

The bank of the river was crowded with families. Children waded in their school shorts. Old men stood with their hands behind their backs. Her aunt handed Hailey the lantern with the name on it, and a man with a long pole steadied it as the candle inside took, and then Hailey crouched at the water's edge and let it go. It spun once, found the current, and joined the others, dozens of them, then hundreds, a slow constellation moving downstream toward the dark. The water was cold on her wrist. Somewhere behind her a mother was telling a small child to say goodbye properly.

On the walk back her phone buzzed. Lila again: so how was the weird summer thing? Hailey stood under a streetlamp with the lantern light still moving behind her eyes, somewhere ahead of her now, going where it was going. She typed: he kept asking about my violin and I never answered. Then she deleted it, because it was not for Lila. She put the phone in her pocket and followed her aunt, who was already several paces on, carrying the empty bucket.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut's dual process model describes grieving people as moving back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with rebuilding daily life, rather than moving in one direction.
story:
The wake was held at Grandmother's house because she had insisted on that years ago, when the insistence was still hypothetical, and nobody in the family had the nerve to overrule her now that it wasn't. Alexandra stood in the kitchen with a paper plate of spanakopita she couldn't finish, watching her aunts move through the rooms like people performing a choreography they'd learned by heart. On the counter sat the blue cardigan, folded, still smelling faintly of lavender and the particular camphor of her grandmother's chest of drawers. Alexandra had decided, on the drive over, that she wanted it. She had not yet managed to pick it up.

Mr. Demetriou from next door came through the screen door with a casserole and a look of gentle embarrassment, the way neighbours do when they aren't sure whether grief makes them welcome or superfluous. He had known Grandmother for forty years and had loved her trenchant opinions about his tomato stakes, which he said kept his garden honest. Alexandra liked him for that, and for the way he said her grandmother's name properly, all three syllables of it, when most people swallowed the last one.

In her pocket her phone buzzed. Gaelle, who had skipped the funeral because her shift at the pool couldn't be covered, was texting in her usual staccato.

"You disappeared. Movie tonight, the theatre by the river, the weird one with the lighthouse. I already bought your ticket. Nonrefundable. I checked."

Alexandra typed back that she was at the house, that there was food, that she wasn't sure she should be anywhere fun this week. Then she put the phone away unfinished, because her mother had appeared in the doorway holding a shoebox of photographs and looking for someone to sit with.

They sat. The photographs were mostly of people Alexandra couldn't name, men in wide collars, a woman on a bicycle with a basket of bread, and her grandmother at nineteen, grinning in a way that made Alexandra's chest hurt. She stayed in that box a long time, and then, without deciding to, she found herself out on the porch with her cousin's plate of honey cake, laughing at Abygael's impression of the priest who'd mispronounced the family name twice in the eulogy. The laugh came out of her like water from a tilted cup, easy and startling, and then it was followed immediately by guilt, which sat in her stomach like a swallowed stone. She put down the cake.

That was when she remembered the letter. Her cousin Dana, away at university, had mailed something a few days after the funeral, and Alexandra had carried it around in her bag, unopened, the way you carry a task you're not ready for. She opened it now under the porch light. Dana wrote about their grandmother too, about the winter she'd taught them both to make the walnut bread, and then, near the end, she wrote something else. In her bereavement seminar, her professor had described the work of Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut, who called it the dual process model. Grieving people, Dana wrote, don't march in one direction through sorrow the way the movies suggest. They swing back and forth, one hour facing the loss directly, the next hour getting on with rebuilding daily life, cooking and laughing and going to the movies, and then back to the loss again. Dana said she wished someone had told her this when their grandfather died, because she had spent that whole spring convinced she was doing it wrong. "It's not betrayal," she'd underlined. "It's the actual mechanism, as far as anyone understands it."

Alexandra read the page twice. The stone in her stomach didn't vanish, exactly, but it grew lighter and less certain of itself, which felt like almost the same thing. She thought of her aunts, one moment weeping over the photographs, the next arguing about whether Grandmother's good pans should go to the church sale, and the swinging between those things stopped looking like failure and started looking like weather. She could not prove Dana's professor was right, and she noticed that she didn't entirely believe the swings would ever settle into anything like peace. What she had was a description that fit, and the honesty to admit that a description is not a cure.

She took out her phone.

"On my way," she wrote to Gaelle. "Save me the seat that doesn't squeak."

Inside, she crossed the kitchen, picked up the blue cardigan, and held it against her face for a long moment, breathing in the lavender and the camphor. Then she folded it over her arm, called to her mother that she'd be back by eleven, and went out through the screen door, which clapped shut behind her twice, the way it always had.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: A pyramid whose base is narrower than its middle shows falling birth rates and an aging population, pointing to rising demand for nursing homes and elder care.
story:
Zoey spread her textbook across her grandmother's kitchen table because the assignment was due first period, and Ms. Yang did not accept late work from anyone, least of all from a girl who had already missed one deadline that semester. The task seemed simple on the surface: choose a country, analyse its population pyramid, and argue whether that country would need more schools or more nursing homes in the coming decades. She had picked her grandmother's birthplace, a small country she had visited twice, because the numbers felt less abstract when she could attach them to a person who cooked her lentils on Sundays.

"Still doing homework at my table," her grandmother said, setting down two glasses of barley water. "You used to do multiplication flashcards there. You cried over the sevens."

"I did not cry." Zoey turned her laptop so the pyramid filled the screen. "I maybe cried once."

She studied the shape. She had assumed it would look like a pyramid, wide at the bottom, narrowing toward the top, the way the textbook's example did. Instead the figure bulged in its middle bands and pinched at its base, like a barrel balanced on a narrow stem. She frowned and checked the axis labels, then checked them again, certain she had misread something. The bars for the youngest age groups were shorter than the bars above them. The base was narrower than the middle.

"What's the matter?" her grandmother asked, peering through her glasses.

"The shape is wrong. It's supposed to be a pyramid." Zoey traced the outline with her finger. "It's telling me fewer babies are being born than there are people in the middle. Falling birth rates." She sat back, letting the implication assemble itself. Fewer births, and that thick middle aging upward year by year. "So the whole thing is getting older. It's going to need nursing homes, not schools." The sentence came out slow, because she was building it as she said it. "A pyramid whose base is narrower than its middle shows falling birth rates and an aging population. That points to rising demand for nursing homes and elder care."

Her grandmother was quiet for a moment, turning her glass on the table. "When I was young there, the schoolyard was so full the children played in shifts. Now my sister writes that they've closed two of them."

A memory surfaced, unbidden: Zoey at nine, standing in that schoolyard during a summer visit, surrounded by cousins and strangers, the noise of it, someone's radio, a game with a flattened ball. It had felt permanent to her, that crowd of children, the way childhood things feel permanent. She had assumed the world she saw was the world that would keep being. Now she understood that the pyramid said otherwise, that the crowd she remembered was the bulge in the middle, moving up.

She opened her draft and began to type, then stopped. Yesterday, before she had looked at the data properly, she had told Pierce she intended to argue for schools. She had a whole angle ready, something inspiring about young populations and building classrooms, and Pierce had said it sounded like a winning thesis. It had felt like artifice even then, a position chosen for its rhetorical shape rather than its evidence, and she had chosen it anyway because it was easier to argue something hopeful. There was something almost atavistic in the hope, she thought, a carryover from flashcard afternoons when the future always meant more of the same, more children, more noise, more of everything growing.

She deleted the paragraph. She had wanted to be the kind of person who defended schools, but the honest answer was elder care, and honesty made a better argument than optimism. Still, a doubt stayed with her as she typed the new thesis. The pyramid showed the shape of the coming decades, but it could not show who would do the caring. If there were fewer young people, who would staff the nursing homes her grandmother's generation would need? She wrote the question into her conclusion and left it there, unanswered, because she did not have an answer and pretending otherwise would be the same artifice in a smaller form.

"Done," she said at last, closing the laptop. Her grandmother had dozed off in the chair beside her, breathing evenly, recuperating from a long shift at the community garden as she recuperated from everything, slowly, in her own time. Zoey watched her for a moment, then reached over and took the empty glass from the table before it could slide off her grandmother's knee.

"Bed, Grandma," she said gently. "You can argue with my conclusion in the morning."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Social loafing, the drop in effort people make in groups, shrinks when each member's individual contribution can be identified.
story:
The rink at six a.m. smelled like cold rubber and burnt coffee from the vending machine, and Owen arrived before anyone else because arriving first was the only thing he could still control. He had been a scratch player for eleven games. The coach said it kindly, the way you tell someone his role is depth, which meant the bench, which meant watching Nash's line take the ice while Owen's legs went stiff beneath the arena's humming lights. He wanted minutes. Not as a gift, not as a courtesy for four years of showing up, but because he had decided sometime in November that if he earned nothing else from this last season, it would be the knowledge that he had earned something.

Nash had been named captain in October, and by January practice had gone soft in a way nobody said out loud. Twenty guys coasting through the drill where the whole squad sprinted the length of the ice together, sticks tapping, everyone moving at the speed of the slowest excuse. Owen felt it happen in his own body, a permission that came from being indistinguishable, one grey jersey among grey jerseys. Mr. Sandhu, who ran the pro shop in the lobby and had watched three decades of teams rotate through, said only one thing to Owen about it, quietly, while sharpening his skates: "Twenty guys, one stopwatch, nobody's name on anything. Do the math on human nature."

The words sat in Owen for a week before they found their shape. He was supposed to be studying for his psychology midterm, half a textbook open on his kitchen table, when he found a passage about social loafing, the drop in effort people make in groups, and how it shrinks when each member's individual contribution can be identified. He read it three times. Then he texted Nash a photo of the page with no caption, and Nash replied forty minutes later with a single line of dialogue that Owen screenshotted without knowing why: "Social loafing. That's us, isn't it."

At the next practice Nash brought a clipboard and a stopwatch and stood at the far blue line calling names one at a time. Each skater sprinted alone, full length, and Nash wrote the time beside his name and read it aloud. The first few times were sloppy. Then Jaida, a winger who had been invisible since November the same way Owen had, laid down a number that made the whole line go quiet, and something shifted in the air like a front moving through. Owen watched guy after guy cross the line bent over, gasping, faces opened up in a way the group sprints never produced. When his own name was called his legs were already shaking, but he thought of the bench, of eleven games of watching, and he skated the fastest lap of his life.

The times went up on the bulletin board by the dressing room the next morning, ranked, each name beside its number. Nobody complained, which surprised Owen. What he had half feared, that the board would enervate the weaker guys, humiliating them into withdrawal, turned out to be backwards. The bottom of the list started arriving earliest. Jaida ran the stairs of the visitor bleachers on off days. Even the veterans who rolled their eyes at Nash's clipboard had stopped straggling in the group drills, as though the stopwatch had gotten inside them and stayed there.

Owen got his minutes in February, six of them in a road game they lost by two, and they felt thinner than he had imagined. He took one shift where nothing happened at all, a slow circle in the defensive zone, and one shift where he forced a turnover at the boards and heard his name come over the PA, and he could not have said which one was the true measure. He kept thinking about the stopwatch, about how being counted had changed everyone, including him, and about whether being counted was the same as mattering. It was an easy epigram and he didn't trust it: what gets measured gets done. His midterm had gone badly. He had spent his study hours photographing a page for Nash.

The day before the last game of the season, Mr. Sandhu waved him over from behind the counter and asked how the board was working out. Owen said the effort had jumped, that it was the strangest thing he'd seen, guys who hadn't cared in December killing themselves in February over a number beside their name. Mr. Sandhu nodded and went back to the skate press, and Owen stood there holding his sticks, unable to decide whether what they'd built was a lever on something real or just a mirror that flattered effort while the game itself stayed out there, unmoved, scored in goals and not in seconds.

In the final period of the final game Owen took a regular shift for the first time all year. With the score tied and under four minutes left, he carried the puck over the red line with his legs burning the way they burned on the timed sprints, and he heard Nash's voice from the bench, hoarse, calling his name, and he looked up at the far blue line where Jaida was breaking open, stick on the ice, and the defenceman was sliding toward Owen, and somewhere behind the glass a stopwatch he could not see was running.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Skimming means reading quickly for the general idea, while scanning means searching a text for one specific detail such as a name or number.
story:
Henry had agreed to it for the money, which he told himself was a reasonable reason and which did not feel like one when Ms. Huang pressed the envelope into his hand at her back door on Tuesday. Inside was twenty dollars, an honorarium, she called it, for reading the local Spanish-language paper and telling her book club what was in it. She had arthritic eyes, she said, and besides, the neighborhood was changing, and she wanted to know it was still being written about somewhere.

Gurman came over on Thursday with his backpack and the smug patience of someone who had survived two years of Señora Okafor. They spread the paper on the kitchen table between Henry's cereal bowl and his mother's unopened mail. The article Ms. Huang had circled was eight paragraphs about a redevelopment plan, and Henry had promised to summarize it aloud on Saturday, in Spanish, in front of twelve retired women who would feed him lemon cake.

"Read it," Gurman said. "Out loud."

Henry began at the first word and proceeded at the speed of a man walking through deep snow. Nouns he recognized. Verbs he guessed at. Every unfamiliar word he stopped for, turned over, looked up on his phone, and by the third paragraph he had been reading for eleven minutes and understood almost nothing.

"Stop." Gurman pulled the phone out of Henry's reach. "What do you actually need here? The general idea, right? For a summary?"

"Obviously."

"Then stop reading word by word. Skimming means reading quickly for the general idea." He slid a finger down the page, fast, barely touching the print. "Headline, first sentences of each paragraph. You're not translating the Bible, you're getting the shape of it."

Henry tried it. His eyes caught proyecto, viviendas, concejo municipal, and out of the drift of unknown words a shape did assemble itself, the way a face assembles out of a crowd. The city council was considering something. Something about housing. His mouth was dry but he said it aloud in clumsy Spanish and Gurman nodded, which was as close to praise as Gurman got.

"There's a date in there somewhere," Henry said. "When they vote. I should know that." He went back to the top and started reading word by word again, carefully, dutifully, the snow-walk, and Gurman made a sound like a punctured tire.

"No. Scanning is when you search a text for one specific detail, like a name or number. You don't read. You hunt." He held the page up. "Dates. Look for numbers. Look for the month names you know. Move your eyes fast and don't stop for anything that isn't a date."

So Henry hunted. His eyes flicked over the gray columns, refusing the trap of sense, looking only for shapes: digits, capitalized months. Septiembre. He found it twice, once near the top and once near the bottom, and it was the second one that slowed him down, because the words around it had begun to arrange themselves without his permission. Demolición. La cuadra entera. The whole block. A list of street names, and his eyes ran down it the way you run your tongue over a cracked tooth, and there, third from the bottom, printed in ordinary ink, was Ms. Huang's street.

He sat back. The kitchen clock ticked. His mother's mail sat on the counter, and somewhere in that pile there was probably a letter about this same thing, some official notice he had carried in from the mailbox without looking.

"What?" Gurman said.

Henry read the paragraph again, slowly now, and this slowness was different from the first; it wasn't the slowness of not knowing but of not wanting to. The redevelopment would replace the old houses on four blocks with new construction, and September was when the council would vote, and there was a public comment session before that, a date he now scanned for and found, because scanning was exactly the right tool and he used it with a sick, competent efficiency.

"She lives on Almendra," he said. "Ms. Huang. Third house. She's lived there since before I was born."

Gurman looked at the list of streets, then at Henry, and had the decency not to say anything reassuring. "What are you going to do?"

The question was the problem. He could summarize the article faithfully on Saturday, in Spanish, standing in Ms. Huang's living room with her twelve friends and the lemon cake, and watch her face while he did it. Or he could walk over tonight and tell her first, privately, in English, so she heard it from a boy she'd paid twenty dollars rather than from a newspaper she couldn't read. Both felt like betrayals of something. He honestly did not know which something.

His mother called from upstairs that dinner was almost ready. Henry folded the paper along its crease and stood at the counter with it under his arm, looking out the dark window toward the yellow light of the house three doors down.

"Give me a minute," he said. "Then I'm going over there."

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), the Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate.
story:
The marble stairs of city hall were still cold at nine in the morning, and Charlie climbed them two at a time with her binder clamped under one arm so the pages could not fan out and reorder themselves. Inside, a woman at a folding table handed her a number, and Charlie sat on a wooden bench beside Jon, who was flipping through his notes with the fake calm of someone who had not slept.

"You drew the school board," he said. "You know that, right? You're against the armbands."

"I know what I drew." She said it quietly, because the hallway was filling with students from three different schools, all of them rehearsing under their breath, and she did not want any of them to hear her argument before she gave it. The case was built on Tinker, the 1969 one, and Ms. Demir had made each of them argue both sides in practice, which was the whole reason Charlie was here at all instead of spending Saturday at Veronica's.

Veronica arrived at 9:15 with coffee for Charlie and none for herself, which was how she apologized for things. "You'll be fine," she said.

"The judges are actual lawyers," Charlie said. "One of them clerks for a real court."

"So don't say anything stupid."

"That's the plan."

The courtroom on the second floor had a low wooden rail and a dais where three judges would sit, and behind the rail there were two tables, one for the petitioner, one for the school board. Jon drew petitioner, which meant he went first, and Charlie listened to him open with the line she had underlined so many times the ink had gone gray: that in 1969, in Tinker v. Des Moines, the Supreme Court ruled 7 to 2 that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate. He said it well. He had a way of letting the second half of a sentence land a half beat late, and when he finished the line the middle judge, a woman with reading glasses pushed up into her hair, nodded once.

When it was Charlie's turn, she stood, straightened the binder she no longer needed, and made herself not look at Jon.

"Counselor, the school board concedes that Tinker exists," she began, and heard a small exhale of laughter from the bench behind the rail, which was what she had wanted. "But Tinker involved silent armbands. My clients' case involves a banner, hung over a stairwell, that named a specific student." She kept her voice level. "The question is not whether rights stop at the schoolhouse gate. The question is what kind of speech the school can regulate once the students are inside it."

The oldest judge leaned forward. "You're asking us to valorize the school's convenience over the students' expression?"

"I'm asking you to weigh a named student's safety against a banner, and I'd argue the balance tips." It was a good answer, incisive enough that Jon, beside her, shifted in his chair. She pressed on through his objections, through the judges' questions, and somewhere in the middle of it she stopped performing the position and started holding it, which frightened her more than the judges did.

Then the middle judge took off her glasses entirely and said, "Counselor, a final question. Do you believe what you just argued?"

The courtroom went still. Behind the rail, Veronica had stopped mid-sip. Charlie's first instinct was the practiced dodge, that her beliefs were not the issue, but the judge was watching her with an expression that had no patience left for contrivance, and Charlie found she could not do it.

"Partly," she said. "I believe schools can regulate speech that targets a student. I don't believe they should get to decide what counts as disruption, and that's the hole in my own side's rule. I stood up here and papered over it because that's the job."

The judge looked at her for a long moment, then at the other two, and wrote something on her pad. Charlie sat down with her heart going hard against her ribs. Jon leaned over under the cover of shuffling papers.

"You just told the judges your argument was wrong."

"I told them where it was wrong. That's different."

"They score on the argument."

"I know how they score."

They called a recess before the ruling, and in the hallway outside the courtroom Veronica found her by the water fountain. "What was that," Veronica said, not really a question.

"Ms. Demir made me argue both sides all month," Charlie said. "I thought it was busywork. Then I got up there and the school's side made sense for the first three minutes, until it didn't, and I couldn't pretend the part where it stopped making sense wasn't there." She drank, because her mouth was dry, and because it gave her something to do with her hands.

"That's either the best thing you've ever done or the worst."

"Probably both."

The doors opened and a student helper called them back in. The three judges were already seated, papers squared in front of them, and the middle judge put on her glasses and looked directly at Charlie's table before she began.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: In the Jewish Passover tradition, the festive meal is called a Seder, a Hebrew word meaning 'order', because its rituals follow a fixed sequence from start to finish.
story:
The Haggadah lay open on the counter between the sink and the stove, its spine cracked at the page for the Four Questions, which was convenient, since Thomas would be singing them tonight in place of his grandfather, who was in the hospital with his hip and had appointed Thomas by phone, in a voice like gravel soaked in broth, as leader of the Seder. Thomas had agreed before he understood what leading meant. It meant knowing which cup to fill and when, when to wash hands, when to break the middle matzah and hide it, when to dip the vegetable in salt water, and it meant doing all of it without stopping to hunt through the book while his younger cousins drummed their spoons and his mother tried to habituate them to patience, which never once in fourteen years of Seders had worked.

He had made index cards. He had made a spreadsheet. He had color-coded the spreadsheet, printed it, and lost the printout somewhere between his backpack and the recycling, and now there were forty minutes until his aunts and uncles arrived, and the kitchen smelled of chicken soup and scorched parsley, because he had left the parsley under the broiler while re-reading the instructions for karpas.

Alina came through the back door without knocking, carrying her chemistry flashcards as an alibi, though she set them on the table and never touched them again. "So walk me through it," she said, hoisting herself onto the counter stool. "You said on the phone you had it handled."

"I have it mostly handled," Thomas said. "The problem is the order. There are like fifteen steps and they're not in the order anyone sensible would put them in. You bless the vegetable before you tell the story, then you tell the story, then you eat the vegetable later? No. Wait. There's a sandwich. There's a sandwich in the middle of a prayer."

Alina picked up the Haggadah and turned it upside down, as if the sequence might arrange itself more sensibly that way. "What does your grandfather do when he forgets?"

"He doesn't forget." Thomas poured himself a glass of water he didn't want. "He's done it since he was younger than me. He could do it in his sleep, and I think he does, kind of. His eyes go somewhere else and his hands just keep going."

He remembered being seven, maybe eight, sitting on the stairs above the dining room while the grownups argued about whether to open a second bottle of wine, and his grandfather had looked up at him, at all the kids on the stairs, and said, you see how we do the same things every year? That's not because we can't think of new things. He hadn't finished the explanation, because Uncle somebody had made a joke about the impecunious state of the family wine budget, and everyone had laughed, and the moment had dissolved, but Thomas had kept the half-finished thought like a coin in a pocket.

Alina was still flipping pages. "Thomas. Look at the cover."

He looked at the cover, which he had looked at his entire life. It said, in Hebrew and then in English, Passover Haggadah, and beneath that, in small type, The Order of the Seder.

"Order," Alina said. "The festive meal itself, the whole thing, is called a Seder, and the word means order."

He stared at her, then at the cover, then at the top of the first page, where the fifteen steps were listed in a rhymed chant he had murmured his whole life without ever hearing what it was saying: kadesh, urchatz, karpas, yachatz. It wasn't that the meal had an order the way a bus schedule has an order. The order was the name of the thing. The sequence from the first cup to the last wasn't scaffolding around the meal; it was the meal, the way a sonnet isn't a bunch of sentences that happen to be fourteen lines long. His spreadsheet had been exactly backwards. He had been trying to memorize steps when what he needed was to stop needing to remember, to let the fixed sequence carry him the way it had carried his grandfather's hands.

"That doesn't solve the parsley," Alina said, nodding at the smoking pan.

By the time the family was seated, Thomas had burned one bunch of parsley and rescued a second, and he had folded the spreadsheet method into something older: he simply began, cup by cup, and when his uncle tried to shortcut the second washing of the hands, Thomas said, "We're doing it in order," and the table, instead of protesting, went quiet and let him, almost relieved, as though they had been waiting years for someone to insist. His youngest cousin found the hidden matzah and held it up for a plebiscite on the reward, and the vote, by show of hands and one fork, was chocolate.

The phone rang near the end of the meal, and his mother brought it to the head of the table and held it to Thomas's ear, and his grandfather's gravel-broth voice said, "So nu, where are you up to?" and Thomas said, "Nirtzah, the last one," and heard the old man sigh, satisfied, and begin, from his hospital bed, four miles away, to sing the closing song a full two bars before the rest of the table could find the tune.
